pages.title: Historical Background
pages.content:
KEY WORDS: Pharaoh, Children of Israel, Exodus, the miracle of the parting of the Red Sea

Moses (pbuh) is one of the great prophets according to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, who saved the Children of Israel from Pharaoh’s despotism. (Pharaohs were the kings of ancient Egypt.) The Children of Israel, or the Israelites, originated from Prophet Jacob (pbuh) and were Jews by birth. Almost the entire Torah consists of the history of Moses (pbuh) and the Israelites under his leadership. Prophet Moses (pbuh) is mentioned 136 times in thirty-four surahs of the Holy Qur’an and is the prophet most frequently mentioned among the prophets in the Qur’an. The Qur’an describes his birth, his arrival at Pharaoh’s palace and his journey to Midian. It also tells of his mission as a prophet, his task to rescue the Children of Israel and his struggle against Pharaoh. Finally, it describes how he led the Children of Israel out of Egypt and guided them. During the time of Prophet Joseph (pbuh), around 1700 BC (BC: Before Christ), the Israelites settled in Egypt. They lived comfortably, rapidly increased in number, and became a large community. However, because they grew so quickly compared to the local population, the Egyptian rulers, who were Copts (ancient Egyptian people), began to see them as a danger. To prevent them from becoming a ruling class, local rulers tried to stop the population growth by making life difficult for the Children of Israel.

exercises.title: Seen as a Danger
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 1 supports.
exercises.question: Why did the Egyptian rulers begin to see the Israelites as a danger?
options: The Israelites had openly demanded to rule Egypt.
The Israelites had grown very quickly compared to the local population.
The Israelites had refused to live alongside the Copts.
exercises.explanation: The end of Chapter 1 gives the cause: “because they grew so quickly compared to the local population, the Egyptian rulers … began to see them as a danger.” Becoming a ruling class was what the rulers feared; the chapter does not say the Israelites demanded it.

feedback.correct: Right. The chapter links the rulers’ fear directly to the Israelites’ rapid growth.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the last two sentences of the chapter and find the sentence that begins with “However, because …”. What exactly worried the rulers?

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Makes the Claim?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the first sentence of Chapter 1. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: “Moses (pbuh) is one of the great prophets according to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam …” — The phrase “according to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam” shows that the writer has proved this as a historical fact.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “According to …” attributes a view to a source. Here the writer reports how three religious traditions see Moses; the phrase frames the claim rather than presenting historical proof. B2 writers use such framing to show whose view a statement expresses.

feedback.correct: Correct. “According to” reports the view of these traditions; it does not present proof.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at the opening sentence. Whose view does “according to …” introduce: The writer’s proof, or the traditions’ view?

languageFocusExercises.title: Cause and Purpose in Other Words
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we give the reason and the aim?

transformItems.source: However, because they grew so quickly compared to the local population, the Egyptian rulers … began to see them as a danger.
transformItems.frame: However, [blank] their rapid growth compared to the local population, the Egyptian rulers … began to see them as a danger.

transformItems.source: To prevent them from becoming a ruling class, local rulers tried to stop the population growth by making life difficult for the Children of Israel.
transformItems.frame: Local rulers tried to stop the population growth by making life difficult for the Children of Israel so that they [blank] a ruling class.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because” is followed by a clause (subject + verb: they grew); “because of / due to” is followed by a noun phrase (their rapid growth). A purpose infinitive such as “to prevent them from becoming …” can be rewritten as a “so that” clause; after a past verb, use “would not / could not + verb”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the cause and the purpose while changing the structure.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: a noun phrase needs “because of” or “due to”. Item 2: after “so that” in the past, use “would not / could not + verb”. Check the end of Chapter 1.

pages.title: Egypt and the Nile
pages.content: As Prophet Isaac (pbuh), Prophet Jacob (pbuh), and Prophet Joseph (pbuh) were their forefathers, the Israelites also believed in their superiority. That is why the pharaohs wanted to keep them weak. According to the sources, Seti I (approximately 1290-1279 BC) was the pharaoh who oppressed the Israelites. Seti I was the father of Ramses II. The Israelites were made to work to build the huge Seti temple during the reign of Seti I and the new capital city of Ramses during the reign of Ramses II. Sources also say that because of the heavy work going on during this time, slaves, including the Israelites, were under a lot of pressure, and this pressure led to trouble and even some protests. As a result of these disorders, the Israelites escaped from Egypt during the rule of Ramses II (approximately 1279-1213 BC). Most of the sources state that the Exodus (Exodus: the departure of the Israelites from Egypt) from Egypt must have taken place in the early thirteenth century BC. So the pharaoh who drowned at sea was probably Ramses II. However, the exact date of the Exodus from Egypt is unknown.

exercises.title: How Sure Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 2 supports.
exercises.question: How certain is the writer that Ramses II was the pharaoh who drowned at sea?
options: Completely certain: The sources prove it beyond doubt.
Fairly sure: It is a likely conclusion, but the exact date of the Exodus is unknown.
Not convinced: The writer names Seti I as the pharaoh who drowned.
Unable to say: The writer reports that no source mentions the Exodus.
exercises.explanation: The writer says, “So the pharaoh who drowned at sea was probably Ramses II,” and adds, “However, the exact date of the Exodus from Egypt is unknown.” “Probably” marks a likely conclusion, not proof. Seti I is named as the pharaoh who oppressed the Israelites, not the one who drowned.

feedback.correct: Yes. “Probably” shows a likely conclusion, and the writer openly admits what is not known.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last three sentences of Chapter 2. Look for the words that show how sure the writer is.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correction.

errorItems.sentence: As a result these disorders, the Israelites escaped from Egypt during the rule of Ramses II (approximately 1279-1213 BC).
The Israelites were made work to build the huge Seti temple during the reign of Seti I …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As a result of + noun phrase” links a consequence to its cause (“As a result of these disorders”). In the active, “make someone work” has no “to”; in the passive, “to” returns: “The Israelites were made to work …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the result phrase and the passive of “make”.
feedback.incorrect: Which small word links “as a result” to a noun? And compare “They made them work” with the passive in Chapter 2.

languageFocusExercises.title: Just as Sure as the Writer
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the summary that says the same as the chapter.
languageFocusExercises.question: “According to the sources, Seti I (approximately 1290-1279 BC) was the pharaoh who oppressed the Israelites.” Which summary is just as sure as the writer?
options: It has been proved beyond doubt that Seti I oppressed the Israelites.
The sources identify Seti I as the pharaoh who oppressed the Israelites.
The writer believes that Seti I did not oppress the Israelites.
Nobody knows which pharaoh oppressed the Israelites.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The original attributes the identification to “the sources”. A faithful summary keeps that attribution; it neither upgrades it to proof nor turns it into the writer’s doubt or into total uncertainty.

feedback.correct: Correct. The summary keeps the claim attributed to the sources.
feedback.incorrect: Notice how the chapter sentence begins. Which summary keeps the claim with the sources, without making it stronger or weaker?

languageFocusExercises.question: What do the sources say, and what is unknown?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The task practises B2 qualification: Evidence can support a conclusion without turning an uncertain point into a fixed fact.

feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “According to the sources”, “probably”, and say one thing that is unknown.
discussionPrompts.example: According to the sources, the Great Wall of China was built over many centuries. Different rulers added new parts to protect their lands. Most of the workers were probably soldiers, farmers and prisoners. The wall was rebuilt many times, so its shape changed. However, the exact number of people who worked on it is unknown.

pages.title: The Pharaoh’s Authority
pages.content: The lands of ancient Egypt have come to life with the fertile waters of the Nile River since the earliest times. The Nile is the source of life for Egypt. Herodotus, the famous historian, points to the importance of this great river with the words, “Egypt is the gift of the Nile.” Control of the Nile River was vital. For this reason, the geographical structure of the land was reshaped by human power. During the reigns of Seti I and Ramses II, canal projects were carried out in the Nile Delta and around it for irrigation, transportation, and commercial purposes. Pharaoh Ramses II, in particular, constructed extensive watering systems (canals) to make agriculture in the delta productive. Thus, Pharaohs undertook huge projects on the river. These projects demanded a vast amount of manpower. Apparently, Pharaohs’ god-king authority was based not only on the richness of the river, but also on the manpower of the slaves, who were forced to work in all kinds of jobs. Just like today’s petrol, control of the power of the Nile also needed a strong administration, a god-king authority.

exercises.title: Two Bases of Power
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 3.
exercises.question: The writer suggests that the Pharaohs’ god-king authority rested only on the richness of the Nile.
exercises.explanation: The writer says the authority “was based not only on the richness of the river, but also on the manpower of the slaves, who were forced to work in all kinds of jobs.” The huge canal projects “demanded a vast amount of manpower.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The writer names two bases of power: The river’s richness and the forced labor of slaves.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence near the end of the chapter that begins with “Apparently”. Does it name one base of power or two?

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does the Analogy Compare?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the last sentence of Chapter 3. Choose what the writer compares.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Just like today’s petrol, control of the power of the Nile also needed a strong administration, a god-king authority.” What does the writer compare?
options: Two dangerous substances that people should keep away from
The way ancient Egyptians used the Nile as a kind of fuel
Two vital resources whose control needs strong, organized power
Modern oil companies and the temples of the pharaohs
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Just like …” introduces an analogy: It compares the function of two things, not the things themselves. Petrol today and the Nile then are both vital resources, and whoever controls them needs strong administration. An analogy clarifies; it does not claim the two are identical.

feedback.correct: Correct. The analogy compares the role of two strategic resources.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what petrol and the Nile have in common in this sentence. Look at the words “control” and “needed a strong administration”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Rebuild the Explanation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say “not only … but also” and “For this reason”?

transformItems.source: Apparently, Pharaohs’ god-king authority was based not only on the richness of the river, but also on the manpower of the slaves …
transformItems.frame: Apparently, Pharaohs’ god-king authority was based on the manpower of the slaves as well as [blank].
answers: on the richness of the river
on the richness of the Nile

transformItems.source: Control of the Nile River was vital. For this reason, the geographical structure of the land was reshaped by human power.
transformItems.frame: Because [blank], the geographical structure of the land was reshaped by human power.
answers: control of the Nile River was vital
control of the Nile was vital
controlling the Nile River was vital

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not only A but also B” gives two bases for power; “B as well as A” keeps both but changes the emphasis. “For this reason” points back to the previous sentence as the cause; “Because + clause” puts the same cause inside one sentence.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept both causes and the cause–consequence link.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: “as well as” needs the other basis of power (the river). Item 2: “Because” needs a full clause with a verb. Check the middle and end of Chapter 3.

languageFocusExercises.title: Like Petrol, but Not the Same
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in 4–6 sentences why the text compares the Nile with petrol.
languageFocusExercises.question: How are the Nile and petrol alike, and how are they different?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 comparison identifies the shared function of strategic resources while respecting the limits of the analogy.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “not only … but also …”, then say how the two are not the same.
discussionPrompts.example: The text compares the Nile with modern petrol because both were sources of great power. The pharaohs’ authority was based not only on the richness of the river but also on the manpower of the slaves. In the same way, a country with petrol needs a strong administration to control it. This is an analogy, not an identity: The Nile was water that gave life, while petrol is a fuel. What they share is the power that comes from controlling them.

pages.title: The Baby in the Water
pages.content: However, Pharaohs had worries about keeping this authority in their hands for a long time. In Moses’ (pbuh) time, the Pharaoh wanted to control the growing population of the Children of Israel in Egypt, while, on the other hand, he regularly ordered the killing of male children born to the Israelites. He heard that the prophet would come from among them. Moses (pbuh) was born into this environment. He was placed in a basket and the basket was set free on the waters of the Nile. It was found at the foot of a tree near the Pharaoh’s palace on the banks of the Nile and he was miraculously saved. The child at the foot of the tree in the waters of the Nile was given the name “Musa” in the Pharaoh’s palace. It was a combination of the words “mu” meaning water, and “sa” meaning tree in the Coptic language (Coptic language: the language spoken by the ancient people of Egypt). The journey of baby Moses began in the waters of the Nile. The river carried him to the Pharaoh’s palace. The salvation of Prophet Moses (pbuh) and his people from the Pharaoh also took place in waters, in the Red Sea.

exercises.title: From the River to the Palace
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 4 in order.
exercises.question: How did baby Moses reach the Pharaoh’s palace?

sequencingItems.text: The Pharaoh regularly ordered the killing of male Israelite babies.
Baby Moses was placed in a basket on the waters of the Nile.
The basket was found at the foot of a tree near the palace.
The child was given the name “Musa” in the Pharaoh’s palace.

exercises.explanation: Moses was born into the danger of the Pharaoh’s order. Then “He was placed in a basket and the basket was set free on the waters of the Nile.” It “was found at the foot of a tree near the Pharaoh’s palace”, and only there was he named “Musa”: “mu” (water) and “sa” (tree) in Coptic.

feedback.correct: Well done. The name came last because it describes where the baby was found: Water and a tree.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the chapter from the beginning to the middle. Where does the name “Musa” come from, and when could it be given?

languageFocusExercises.title: Why Not Say Who Did It?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 4. Choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “He was placed in a basket and the basket was set free on the waters of the Nile.” Why does the writer not say who did these actions?
options: To show that nobody actually did these actions
To keep attention on the baby and the basket rather than on the person who acted
To show that Moses did these actions himself
To describe actions that will happen later in the story
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive (be + past participle) puts the person or thing affected at the start of the clause. The chapter is about what happens to baby Moses, so the unnamed actor is not important here. A passive does not mean that no one acted.

feedback.correct: Correct. The passive keeps Moses and the basket at the center of the narrative.
feedback.incorrect: Who or what is the subject of each clause? Is the writer interested in who acted, or in what happened to the baby?

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake in the verb. Tap it, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the verbs that say what happened?

errorItems.sentence: It was find at the foot of a tree near the Pharaoh’s palace on the banks of the Nile and he was miraculously saved.
The child at the foot of the tree in the waters of the Nile was give the name “Musa” in the Pharaoh’s palace.
The salvation of Prophet Moses (pbuh) and his people from the Pharaoh also was taken place in waters, in the Red Sea.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive needs be + past participle: “was found”, “was given”. (“Founded” is the past of “found” = establish.) “Take place” is intransitive, so it has no passive: “also took place”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You formed two passives and kept “take place” active.
feedback.incorrect: Use the past participle after “was” (find → found, give → given). “Take place” never takes the passive. Check the middle and end of Chapter 4.

Later, he and his people were saved from the Pharaoh in the waters of the Red Sea. While the first water took him into the Pharaoh’s house, the second took his people out of the Pharaoh’s power.

pages.title: The Pharaoh’s Command
pages.content: As a tyrant, the Pharaoh ruled Egypt with absolute power over the people. He oppressed the Children of Israel, known as the offspring of Prophet Jacob (pbuh). He used every method to dishonor them. The Pharaoh made the Children of Israel work under extremely heavy conditions for small pay or no money. Under these circumstances, people obeyed the Pharaoh. He saw himself as a god. It is possible that some people of that period did not practise or believe in paganism. But they kept it secret and outwardly followed social norms without opposing the Pharaoh or telling who they were because they were weak. Years passed, and the despotic kings continued to rule Egypt. One day, the Pharaoh had a vision that one of the Israelite sons would take him down from his throne. Ibn Abbas said, “The Pharaoh saw a fire in his vision. The fire came from Jerusalem and burned the houses of the Egyptians, but did not do any harm to the Children of Israel.” When he woke up, he called all his priests and magicians and asked about the dream. They said, “A boy will be born among the Children of Israel, and the Egyptian people will die at this boy’s hands.”

The Pharaoh “saw himself as a god.” For the people who hid their belief, the writer is careful: “It is possible that …”, and they stayed silent “because they were weak.” The vision is reported with “Ibn Abbas said,” and the prediction comes from the priests and magicians: “A boy will be born among the Children of Israel …”

feedback.correct: Good. You kept each claim with its source, including the writer’s careful “It is possible that …”.
feedback.incorrect: Check who speaks or is described in each part: The middle of the chapter for the Pharaoh and the people who kept quiet, the end for the vision and its meaning.

outwardly followed social norms

The Pharaoh made the Children of Israel to work under extremely heavy conditions for small pay or no money.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter only says “It is possible that …”; “certain”, “clear” or “obvious” would overclaim. In the active, make + object + bare infinitive expresses forced action: “made the Children of Israel work”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reporting the Vision
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Report each quotation from Chapter 5. Write only the missing words.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happens to “saw” and “will be” when you report them?

transformItems.source: Ibn Abbas said, “The Pharaoh saw a fire in his vision. …”
transformItems.frame: Ibn Abbas said that the Pharaoh [blank] a fire in his vision.

transformItems.source: They said, “A boy will be born among the Children of Israel, and the Egyptian people will die at this boy’s hands.”
transformItems.frame: They said that a boy [blank] born among the Children of Israel, and the Egyptian people would die at this boy’s hands.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, the past simple usually moves back to the past perfect (“had seen”, though “saw” is also accepted), and “will” becomes “would”. feedback.correct: Well done. You reported the vision and the prediction with the right tenses.

discussionPrompts.question: Say who said it, use “said that …”, and keep the prediction apart from facts.

So our school is preparing, but nobody can say for sure that the flood will come.

pages.title: A Baby in the Nile
pages.content: Then the Pharaoh commanded that all the male children of Israel should be killed. His men carried out the order. But the Pharaoh began to lose his manpower because the Children of Israel did most of the heavy jobs in the country. His economic experts warned him and offered a solution. According to the new policy, his men would kill male children in one year, but let them live in the next year. The Pharaoh thought the solution was economically realistic, so he accepted it. Moses was born in a year in which boys were to be killed. His mother was very frightened by his birth, so she nursed him in secret for fear that he would be killed. Allah said: “…We inspired the mother of Moses, saying: ‘Suckle him (Moses), but when you fear for him, then put him into the river and fear not, nor grieve. Verily! We shall bring him back to you, and shall make him one of (Our) Messengers.’” (Surah al-Qasas: 7) Moses’ mother had to put the baby into a basket and throw it into the waters of the Nile. She was so sad, but she knew that Allah was much kinder to baby Moses than she was.

exercises.title: An Economic Decision
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 6 supports.
exercises.question: Why did the Pharaoh change his order to kill all male Israelite babies?
options: His priests told him that the vision had been false.
He was losing the workers who did most of the heavy jobs.
Queen Asiye persuaded him to stop the killing.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says, “the Pharaoh began to lose his manpower because the Children of Israel did most of the heavy jobs in the country.” His economic experts suggested killing boys in one year and sparing them in the next, and he accepted it because it was “economically realistic”. The change was about labor, not mercy.

feedback.correct: Right. The reason was economic: he needed the Israelites’ labor.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first five sentences of Chapter 6. What did the economic experts warn the Pharaoh about?

languageFocusExercises.title: Instruction and Reassurance
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each part of the Qur’anic words in Chapter 6 with what it does.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does each part tell Moses’ mother?

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The quoted passage moves from a condition (“when you fear for him, then …”) to an instruction, a comforting prohibition (“fear not, nor grieve”), and two promises with “shall”. The order turns a frightening instruction into reassurance.

feedback.correct: Correct. You identified condition, prohibition and the two promises.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the quotation in Chapter 6. Which part tells her when to act, which part forbids a feeling, and which parts promise the future?

languageFocusExercises.title: Cause, Result and Fear
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 6 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: But the Pharaoh began to lose his manpower [blank] the Children of Israel did most of the heavy jobs in the country. … The Pharaoh thought the solution was economically realistic, [blank] he accepted it. … His mother was very frightened by his birth, so she nursed him in secret [blank] that he would be killed.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because” introduces the cause of the lost manpower. “So” introduces the result of the Pharaoh’s judgement. “For fear that + clause” gives the danger an action tries to avoid. “In case” is not followed by “that”, and “although” would signal a contrast the chapter does not make.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the linkers for cause, result and feared danger.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Does the next clause give a reason, a result, or something she was afraid of? Check the first and last paragraphs of Chapter 6.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explaining a Difficult Decision
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Describe a hard decision in five sentences.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why was the decision hard, and what was promised?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: B2 use means combining forms into a coherent decision sequence rather than practising them in isolation.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use a reason, “if” or “when”, an instruction, and a promise with “will”.
discussionPrompts.example: My neighbor had to send her son to a school in another city because the school in our town had closed. It was a hard decision, as he was only fifteen. She told him, “If you feel lonely, call me every evening.” She also asked his new teacher to keep an eye on him. Then she said, “You will come home every holiday, and we will be together again.”

pages.title: Queen Asiye’s Love
pages.content: Allah was their Lord and also the Lord of the Nile. Allah commanded the waves to be calm and gentle while carrying the baby. The basket came to the shore near the Pharaoh’s palace. The palace servants noticed the basket and took it to the Pharaoh and the queen Asiye. When Queen Asiye saw the baby, she felt a strong love for him in her heart. The queen was a good and kind-hearted woman who, unlike her husband, held a belief in Allah. She was a secret believer and persuaded her husband with her words that this baby would be a ray of light for both of them! (see Surah al-Qasas: 9) She was always sad because she was sterile. She said to her husband, “Let me keep the baby and let him be our son.” The Pharaoh accepted it. Then, she said to her servants, “Find a nurse for the baby.” Moses’ mother heard the news, too. While the queen was trying to choose a wet nurse to feed the baby, Moses’ mother was also waiting with a heavy heart.

exercises.title: Queen Asiye
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 7 supports.
exercises.question: Why was Queen Asiye always sad before the baby came to the palace?
options: She had lost a son because of the Pharaoh’s order.
She could not have children of her own.
The Pharaoh had refused to let her keep a child.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says, “She was always sad because she was sterile,” which means she could not have children. This helps explain her words to the Pharaoh: “Let me keep the baby and let him be our son.”

feedback.correct: Yes. She had no children, so the baby answered a deep wish of her heart.
feedback.incorrect: Look in the middle of Chapter 7 for a sentence with “because”. What was the reason for the queen’s sadness?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Hope Reported from the Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 7 and choose the best explanation of “would be”.
languageFocusExercises.question: “She was a secret believer and persuaded her husband with her words that this baby would be a ray of light for both of them!” What does “would be” show?
options: A fact about the baby that the narrator has already proved
A past habit of the baby in the palace
Asiye’s hopeful prediction, reported from a past point in the story
A polite request that Asiye makes to the Pharaoh
languageFocusExercises.explanation: After a past reporting verb (“persuaded … that”), “will be” becomes “would be”. The narrator reports Asiye’s argument about the future from her point of view in the past; it is her persuasive framing, not a proven fact.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Would be” reports Asiye’s view of the future from a past moment.
feedback.incorrect: Who is making this claim, and when? Notice the reporting verb “persuaded … that” before “would be”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Report the Request, Keep the Contrast
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we report her words and show a difference?

transformItems.source: She said to her husband, “Let me keep the baby and let him be our son.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A request with “Let me …” is reported as “asked + person + to let her …” or “asked if she could …”. A command is reported with “told + person + to + verb”. “Unlike + noun” becomes a clause with “whereas / while / but” when both sides have their own verb.

feedback.correct: Well done. You reported the request and the command and rebuilt the contrast.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: “asked her husband to let her …” or “asked if she could …”. Item 2: “told + person + to + verb”. Item 3: a contrast linker before a full clause. Check Chapter 7.

pages.title: Moses Grows Up
pages.content: When the baby took her breast, he immediately started suckling. The Pharaoh was astonished and asked, “Who are you? This child refused the milk of all other women but yours.” Allah gave her inner strength, and she answered, “I have sweet milk and a sweet scent, so no baby refuses me.” This answer pleased the Pharaoh. She continued to feed him for a long time. Thus, baby Moses would grow up in his mother’s arms. Moses was raised as a prince in the palace. Moses became a young man. He had not yet been given the prophetic mission. He couldn’t decide whether he should be thankful to the Pharaoh or oppose the oppression against the Children of Israel. Allah gave Moses perfect health, strength, wisdom, and knowledge. Because of these gifts, the weak and oppressed always looked to him for protection and justice. One day in the main town, he noticed two men fighting. One of them was an Israelite and the other was an Egyptian. Young Moses felt close to the Israelites because he had come from the water, not from a noble family, and his mother was one of the Children of Israel.

languageFocusExercises.title: Timeline: Not Yet
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 8. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: “He had not yet been given the prophetic mission.” — This sentence means that, at this point in the story, Moses was already a prophet but had not started preaching.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Had not yet been given” (past perfect passive + “not yet”) says that by this point the mission had not happened; it comes later. The young man’s inner conflict belongs to the time before prophethood.

errorItems.sentence: He couldn’t decide whether should he be thankful to the Pharaoh or oppose the oppression against the Children of Israel.
Because these gifts, the weak and oppressed always looked to him for protection and justice.

pages.title: The Warning
pages.content: Upon seeing Moses, the man from the Children of Israel begged him for help. Thus, Moses got involved in the dispute and angrily hit the Egyptian who instantly died. He unintentionally killed the Copt with a single punch. Moses was filled with fear and sadness. He immediately turned to Allah to ask for forgiveness. The very next day, Moses saw the same Israelite involved in another dispute. Moses understood that the Israelite was a quarrelsome man. Moses approached him. Fearing Moses might harm him, the man reacted with a shout, “Will you kill me just as you killed that Egyptian yesterday?” The news thus spread among the Egyptians. Moses was aware that killing an Egyptian would result in the death penalty. So Moses’ fear was not unreasonable. A man of faith who came from the palace warned him, “Run away, or the Pharaoh will kill you for this crime.” Moses was forced to leave Egypt.

exercises.title: A Reasonable Fear
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 9 supports.

The Pharaoh’s soldiers had already arrested him in the town.
Moses had planned the fight with the Egyptian in advance.
exercises.explanation: The chapter reasons step by step: “The news thus spread among the Egyptians. Moses was aware that killing an Egyptian would result in the death penalty. So Moses’ fear was not unreasonable.” The killing itself was not planned: “He unintentionally killed the Copt with a single punch.”

feedback.correct: Right. The writer’s judgement rests on two facts: The punishment for the killing and the spreading news.
feedback.incorrect: Find the sentence that begins with “So Moses’ fear …” in the middle of Chapter 9, then read the two sentences just before it.

languageFocusExercises.title: Action and Consequence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the phrases from Chapter 9: a choice someone made, or what followed?

angrily hit the Egyptian

who instantly died

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter separates what Moses chose to do from what followed. “Unintentionally” makes clear that the death was not his aim; “thus” and “was forced to” mark consequences. B2 readers keep intention and outcome apart.

feedback.correct: Correct. You kept the chosen actions separate from their consequences.

languageFocusExercises.title: Intention, Result and Warning
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say “unintentionally”, “result in” and “Run away, or …”?

transformItems.source: He unintentionally killed the Copt with a single punch.
transformItems.frame: He killed the Copt with a single punch, but he did not [blank] to.

transformItems.source: Moses was aware that killing an Egyptian would result in the death penalty.

transformItems.source: A man of faith who came from the palace warned him, “Run away, or the Pharaoh will kill you for this crime.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Unintentionally” = “did not mean/intend to”. “A results in B” means the same as “B results from A”: the preposition changes when the order changes. “Imperative + or + consequence” is a warning that means “If you do not …, …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept intention, result and warning while changing the structure.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: which verb means “have the intention”? Item 2: result in → result from when you swap the order. Item 3: “Run away, or …” means “If you do not run away, …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Serious, Even If Not Planned

languageFocusExercises.question: Is harm less serious if nobody planned it?

pages.title: A Prayer for Forgiveness
pages.content: Allah related: “And he entered the city at a time of unawareness of its people, and he found there two men fighting, one of his party (his religion, from the Children of Israel), and the other of his enemy. The man of his own party asked him for help against his enemy, so Moses struck him with his fist and killed him.” He said: “My Lord! Verily, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.” Then He forgave him. Verily, He is the Forgiving, the Most Merciful. He said: “My Lord! For that with which You have favored me, I will never more be a helper for the criminals (those disobedient to Allah, polytheists, sinners, etc.)!” So, he became afraid, looking about in the city, waiting as to what would be the result of his crime of killing, when behold, the man who had sought his help the day before called for his help again. Moses said to him: “Verily, you are a plain troublemaker!” Then, when he decided to seize the man who was an enemy to both of them, the man said: “O Moses! Is it your intention to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? Your aim is nothing but to become a tyrant in the land, and not to be one of those who do right.”

pages.title: Escape to Midian
pages.content: And there came a man running from the farthest end of the city (from the palace). He said: “O Moses! Verily, the chiefs are taking counsel together about you to kill you, so escape. Truly, I am to you one of those who give sincere advice.” So he escaped from there, looking about in a state of fear. He said: “My Lord! Save me from the people who are wrongdoers!” (Surah al-Qasas: 15-21) Moses (pbuh) hurried out of Egypt without changing his clothes or getting prepared for traveling. He headed for the land of Midian, which was the closest inhabited area between Egypt and Syria. It was a region not ruled by the Pharaoh. His only companion in this hot desert was Allah and his trust in Him. The hot sand burned his soles. However, fearing pursuit by the Pharaoh’s men, he forced himself to continue on. He traveled by night, hiding during the day. After his desert journey, he reached a watering hole outside Midian. He found shepherds there with their flocks.

pages.title: The Women Shepherds
pages.content: He immediately began to seek rest under a tree, exhausted and hungry. The bottoms of his feet were raw. They were worn out from hard walking on sand and rocks and from the dust. He urgently needed a new pair of sandals, food and drink. While at a well in Midian, Moses saw a group of shepherds and noticed two young women who were trying to get water for their flocks. Due to the crowd at the water source, the young women could only water their animals after the male shepherds had taken their flocks away. Moses noticed their hardship and sensed that the women were in need of help. Forgetting his thirst, Moses approached them and asked if he could help them in any way. The older sister said, “We are waiting until the shepherds finish watering their sheep, then we will water ours.” Moses was surprised that women were shepherding. It was hard and tiresome work. He asked, “Why are you shepherding?” The younger sister said, “Our father is an old man; his health is too poor and he cannot go out to shepherd the flock.”

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “could only … after” Show?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 12 and choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Due to the crowd at the water source, the young women could only water their animals after the male shepherds had taken their flocks away.” What does the sentence tell us?
options: The women watered their animals first and then the men watered theirs.

The women refused to water their animals because of the crowd.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Could only … after …” limits the action to one time: Not before the men had finished. “Due to + noun” gives the cause of the limit, and the past perfect “had taken” shows the men’s action came first.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Only … after” makes the waiting a restriction, not a choice.

pages.title: Shu’ayb’s Home
pages.content: Moses said, “I will water the sheep for you.” He watered their sheep. He went back to sit in the shade of the tree. He suddenly realized he hadn’t drunk any water. He was also so hungry that his stomach ached from hunger. The father of these girls was Prophet Shu’ayb (pbuh). Prophet Shu’ayb (pbuh) was sent as a messenger of Allah to the eastern part of the Gulf of Aqaba, that is, Midian. Being very old, Prophet Shu’ayb (pbuh) had to send the girls alone with animals. The young ladies returned home unexpectedly early, which surprised their father. Due to Moses’ help at the spring, they came back early and told him about it. Their father sent one of his daughters to invite the stranger to his home. She went up to Moses and said that her father was grateful for his help. She said, “Our father invites you to our home so that he may thank you in person.” Moses welcomed this invitation and followed the maiden back to her father. It was clear to Moses that they enjoyed a comfortable and harmonious home life. After introducing himself, he told him about the unfortunate events in Egypt that had forced him to escape.

pages.title: A Shepherd’s Life
pages.content: The old man comforted him, “Do not fear, you have escaped from the wrongdoers.” The father and his daughters observed Moses’ gentleness. Shu’ayb (pbuh) invited him to stay with them. Moses felt at home with this family, for they were friendly and believed in Allah. Because they needed someone reliable and strong, one of the daughters advised her father to employ Moses. They offered Moses work with them. This offer suited Moses well because he was a stranger in this country and urgently needed shelter and work. Moses became a shepherd for the family, married one of the daughters of the old man, and looked after the old man’s animals for ten long years. Time passed, and he spent much of his time in deep thought in the middle of the desert, far from his people. This period of ten years was important in his life. It was a period of spiritual preparation for prophethood. After a period of ten years, Moses returned to his fatherland, Egypt, during the early days of Ramses II’s rule (approximately 1279-1213 BC). Moses left Midian with his family and was returning to Egypt across the Sinai.

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose, Duration and Time
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 14 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: This period of ten years was important in his life. It was a period of spiritual preparation [blank] prophethood. [blank] a period of ten years, Moses returned to his fatherland, Egypt, [blank] the early days of Ramses II’s rule (approximately 1279-1213 BC).
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Preparation for” names what the period prepares him for. “After a period of ten years” marks the end of the period. “During + noun” places his return inside a longer time span; “while” would need a clause, and “since” would need a perfect tense.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the prepositions for purpose, sequence and time span.
feedback.incorrect: Check what follows each gap: A noun (prophethood), a length of time, and a noun phrase (the early days). Compare with the end of Chapter 14.

languageFocusExercises.title: Preparation or Delay?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in 6–7 sentences why the ten years were preparation, not delay.
languageFocusExercises.question: Were the ten years in Midian wasted time?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: B2 interpretation should be explicitly tied to textual evidence and framed as the text’s interpretation.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Give two facts from the chapter, and use “The chapter presents …”.
discussionPrompts.example: The chapter presents the ten years in Midian as a time of growth, not as wasted time. First, it says that Moses (pbuh) spent much of his time in deep thought in the middle of the desert. Second, it states directly that this was a period of spiritual preparation for prophethood. A delay would mean waiting with no purpose. Here, however, the years are linked to his future mission. He also found shelter, work and a family. For these reasons, “preparation” fits the text better than “delay”.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: When did Moses (pbuh) return to Egypt?

during the early days of Ramses II’s rule

pages.title: The Voice at Mount Sinai
pages.content: They traveled through the desert until they reached Mount Sinai. It was winter. There, Moses discovered that he had lost his way. He sought Allah’s direction, and Allah showed him the right course. At nightfall, they reached Mount Sinai, also known as Mount Tur. Moses noticed a fire in the distance and approached it, hoping to bring his family some fire to warm themselves and find a guide by the fire. As he neared the fire, he heard a thundering voice calling him: “O Moses, I am Allah, the Lord of the Universe.” Moses was shocked and looked around. He again heard the strange voice: “And what is in your right hand, O Moses?” Moses trembled and responded, “This is my staff on which I lean, and I use it to cut branches for my sheep.” Allah asked about the staff in Moses’ hand to make him focus on it. In this way Allah was preparing him for the miracle that was about to happen. This was the beginning of Moses’ mission as a prophet. The same voice told him, “Throw down your staff!” He did so, and at once the staff became a twisting snake. Moses began to run, but the voice again said to him, “Do not fear and hold it; We will make it a staff.”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:moses-mount-sinai
The time in the evening when it becomes dark.
Extremely loud and deep, like a storm.
To shake because of fear or strong feeling.
A long wooden stick used for support when walking.
Turning and bending from side to side.

hotspots.title: A Fire in the Distance
hotspots.description: Lost on a winter night, Moses (pbuh) walked toward a fire, hoping to find warmth and a guide.

hotspots.title: The Staff Becomes a Snake
hotspots.description: When Moses (pbuh) threw down his staff, it became a twisting snake.

exercises.title: Why the Question?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 15 supports.
exercises.question: According to the writer, why did Allah ask Moses what was in his right hand?
options: to test whether Moses had lost his way in the desert
to make Moses focus on the staff and prepare him for the miracle
to tell Moses to leave the staff with his family
exercises.explanation: After Moses answers, the writer explains: “Allah asked about the staff in Moses’ hand to make him focus on it. In this way Allah was preparing him for the miracle that was about to happen.” Then the staff became a snake.

feedback.correct: Yes. The question drew Moses’ attention to the staff just before it became a sign.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentences right after Moses answers, “This is my staff …”. The writer explains the purpose there.

languageFocusExercises.title: Hoping, Not Achieving
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 15 and choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Moses noticed a fire in the distance and approached it, hoping to bring his family some fire to warm themselves and find a guide by the fire.” What does “hoping to …” show?
options: A result he wanted but could not yet be sure of
Something he had already done before he saw the fire
An order that someone gave him
Something he used to do every winter
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The participle phrase “hoping to + verb” adds Moses’ aim at the moment he moves: warmth and guidance. “Hoping” marks an uncertain, wished-for result. The chapter then turns this ordinary purpose into the beginning of his mission.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Hoping to” expresses a purpose that is not yet certain.
feedback.incorrect: Notice the word “hoping”. Did Moses already have the fire and a guide, or did he want them?

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose and Something About to Happen
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say “to make him” and “about to happen”?

transformItems.source: Allah asked about the staff in Moses’ hand to make him focus on it.
transformItems.frame: Allah asked about the staff in Moses’ hand so that he [blank] on it.

transformItems.source: In this way Allah was preparing him for the miracle that was about to happen.
transformItems.frame: In this way Allah was preparing him for the miracle that [blank] happen very soon.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A purpose infinitive (“to make him focus”) can become a “so that” clause; in a past context use “would / could + verb”. “Was about to happen” means it was going to happen very soon: A future seen from a past moment, which signals the coming turning point.

feedback.correct: Well done. You rewrote the purpose and the near future in the past.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: after “so that” in the past, use “would” or “could”. Item 2: “about to” = “going to … very soon”, in the past. Check the second half of Chapter 15.

languageFocusExercises.title: Ordinary → Extraordinary
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Describe in five sentences how the staff goes from ordinary to amazing.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does a simple stick become part of a miracle?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The task practises discourse movement from familiar description to a transformed meaning.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “At first”, “Then”, and “which” or “on which”.
discussionPrompts.example: At first, the staff is an ordinary tool on which Moses (pbuh) leans. He also uses it to cut branches for his sheep. Then Allah asks him about the staff, which makes him focus on it. When he throws it down, it becomes a twisting snake. In this way, a simple shepherd’s stick becomes part of a miracle.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Moses (pbuh) say he used his staff for?
options: to lean on and to cut branches for his sheep
beforeYouRead.quote: This is my staff on which I lean, and I use it to cut branches for my sheep.

I can describe how an ordinary thing becomes extraordinary.

pages.title: The Two Signs
pages.content: The snake changed back into his staff. Moses’ fear subsided, and he felt peace because he realized that he was witnessing the Truth. Then, Allah commanded him to place his hand under his arm. When he pulled it out, the hand was exceptionally shiny! The miracle of the staff and the miracle of the white hand given to Prophet Moses (pbuh) were two great miracles. Allah then commanded Moses: “You have two signs from your Lord; go to Pharaoh and his chiefs, for they are an evil group and have violated all limits.” Allah narrated this event: “And has there come to you the story of Moses? When he saw a fire, he said to his family: ‘Wait! Verily, I have seen a fire; perhaps I can bring you some burning brand therefrom, or find some guidance at the fire.’ And when he came to the fire, he was called by name: ‘O Moses! Verily! I am your Lord! So take off your shoes; you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa. And I have chosen you. So listen to that which is inspired to you. Verily! I am Allah! La ilaha illa Ana (none has the right to be worshipped but I), so worship Me, and offer prayers perfectly for My remembrance.”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:moses-valley-of-tuwa
__historical_entity__:moses-pharaoh
To become less strong and gradually go away.
To see something important happen with your own eyes.
Unusually; to a very high degree.
The most powerful leaders of a people.
Holy; deserving special respect because it is connected with God.

hotspots.title: The Shining Hand
hotspots.description: Moses’ (pbuh) hand came out white and shining: The second of his two great signs.

hotspots.title: The Valley of Tuwa
hotspots.description: Allah told Moses (pbuh) to take off his shoes because he was standing in the sacred valley.

exercises.title: From Fear to Peace
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 16.
exercises.question: Moses’ fear subsided when the snake turned back into a staff because he realized that he was witnessing the Truth.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says: “The snake changed back into his staff. Moses’ fear subsided, and he felt peace because he realized that he was witnessing the Truth.” After the second sign, the shining hand, he was sent to “Pharaoh and his chiefs.”

feedback.correct: Correct. His fear changed into peace because he understood that the sign came from the Truth.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first two sentences of Chapter 16 again. What happened to Moses’ fear, and why?

languageFocusExercises.title: At the Fire: What the Words Do
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each Qur’anic line in Chapter 16 with what it does.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does each quoted line do in the scene at the fire?

matchingPairs.left: ‘Wait! Verily, I have seen a fire …’
matchingPairs.right: tells his family to stay where they are while he goes on

matchingPairs.left: perhaps I can bring you some burning brand therefrom
matchingPairs.right: offers a hopeful possibility, not a promise

matchingPairs.left: So take off your shoes; you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa.

matchingPairs.left: so worship Me, and offer prayers perfectly for My remembrance

correctAnswer.‘Wait! Verily, I have seen a fire …’: tells his family to stay where they are while he goes on
correctAnswer.perhaps I can bring you some burning bra: offers a hopeful possibility, not a promise
correctAnswer.So take off your shoes; you are in the s: gives an instruction and then the reason for it
correctAnswer.so worship Me, and offer prayers perfect: draws a consequence from the declaration that only Allah is to be worshipped

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Perhaps I can …” softens a plan into a possibility. In “take off your shoes; you are in the sacred valley”, the second clause gives the reason for the command. “So worship Me” follows from “none has the right to be worshipped but I”: “so” marks the consequence.

feedback.correct: Correct. You identified the request, the possibility, the reasoned command and the consequence.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the quotation in Chapter 16. Look for “perhaps”, for the clause after the semicolon, and for what comes before “so worship Me”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reason and Reported Command
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say “because he realized” and Allah’s command?

transformItems.source: Moses’ fear subsided, and he felt peace because he realized that he was witnessing the Truth.
transformItems.frame: [blank] that he was witnessing the Truth, Moses felt his fear subside and felt peace.

transformItems.source: Allah then commanded Moses: “You have two signs from your Lord; go to Pharaoh and his chiefs, for they are an evil group and have violated all limits.”
transformItems.frame: Allah then commanded Moses [blank] to Pharaoh and his chiefs because they were an evil group.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A because-clause can be shortened into a participle clause when the subject is the same: “Realizing that …, Moses …”. A reported command uses command + object + to-infinitive: “commanded Moses to go”. “For” in the quotation means “because”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You compressed the reason and reported the command.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: start with an -ing form of “realize” (or a because-clause). Item 2: commanded + person + to + verb. Check Chapter 16.

languageFocusExercises.title: Evidence Creates Responsibility
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in 5–7 sentences how the two signs change Moses’ life.
languageFocusExercises.question: How is Moses different after the two signs?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The B2 target is to integrate grammar with the chapter’s meaning: Signs are followed by a public responsibility.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “because …”, “commanded him to …” and “so that …”.
discussionPrompts.example: Before the signs, Moses (pbuh) was a shepherd traveling with his family. His fear subsided because he realized that he was witnessing the Truth. He was given the staff and the white hand so that he would have clear signs from his Lord. Allah then commanded him to go to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Now he had evidence, and with it came a great responsibility. He was no longer only a shepherd; he had a mission.

beforeYouRead.quote: When he pulled it out, the hand was exceptionally shiny!

pages.title: The Mission Begins
pages.content: Allah also said: “Verily, the Hour is coming - and My Will is to keep it hidden - that every person may be rewarded for what he strives for. Therefore, do not let him who denies it (the Day of Resurrection, Paradise, and Hell, etc.) and follows his own desires turn you away from it, lest you fall. And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?” He said: “This is my stick, I lean on it, and with it I beat down branches for my sheep and I find other uses in it.” Allah said: “Cast it down, O Moses!” He cast it down, and behold! It was a snake, moving quickly. Allah said: “Hold it, and fear not. We shall return it to its former state, and press your right hand to your left side; it will appear white and shining, and without any disease, as another sign, that We may show you some of Our greater signs. Go to Pharaoh! Verily! He has gone beyond all limits (all bounds in disbelief and disobedience, and has behaved as an arrogant tyrant).” (Surah Taha: 9-24) The religion of Moses (pbuh) was the same as that of Jacob (pbuh), which was Islamic monotheism. His forefather was Jacob (pbuh), the grandson of Abraham (pbuh). Moses (pbuh), therefore, was one of the descendants of Abraham (pbuh), and every prophet who came after Abraham (pbuh) was one of Abraham’s successors.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:moses-pharaoh
The belief that there is only one God.
A person who comes from a particular ancestor in a later generation.
Someone who comes after another person and continues their work.
Strong wishes, especially for things that please oneself.
Belonging to an earlier time; previous.

hotspots.title: “Go to Pharaoh!”
hotspots.description: Allah sent Moses (pbuh) to the Pharaoh, who had gone beyond all limits.

hotspots.title: In Abraham’s Line
hotspots.description: Moses (pbuh) came from Jacob (pbuh), the grandson of Abraham (pbuh), and followed the same belief in One God.

exercises.title: The Last Paragraph
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 17 supports.
exercises.question: After the long Qur’anic passage, what is the main point of the last part of Chapter 17?
options: Moses’ religion was the same monotheism as Jacob’s, which places him in Abraham’s line of prophets.
Moses brought a new religion that was different from the religion of Jacob.
Moses was the grandson of Abraham and the forefather of Jacob.
Aaron was chosen to go to the Pharaoh instead of Moses.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says, “The religion of Moses (pbuh) was the same as that of Jacob (pbuh), which was Islamic monotheism.” Jacob was “the grandson of Abraham,” so Moses was one of Abraham’s descendants, and “every prophet who came after Abraham (pbuh) was one of Abraham’s successors.”

feedback.correct: Right. The paragraph shows continuity: One message of monotheism passed down through Abraham’s line.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last three sentences of Chapter 17, after “(Surah Taha: 9-24)”. How are Moses, Jacob and Abraham connected?

languageFocusExercises.title: Warning: “lest”
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the Qur’anic line from Chapter 17 and choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Therefore, do not let him who denies it … turn you away from it, lest you fall.” What does “lest you fall” mean?
options: so that you do not fall
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Lest” is a formal word that introduces the danger an action should prevent: “lest you fall” = “so that you do not fall / in case you fall”. With “Therefore” and “do not let …”, the line forms a warning: a consequence, a prohibition, and the danger to avoid.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Lest” introduces the result the warning tries to prevent.
feedback.incorrect: The line warns Moses not to be turned away. Is falling the aim, a time limit, or the danger to avoid?

languageFocusExercises.title: The Language of Continuity
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct words for each sentence from Chapter 17.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the chapter link Moses to Jacob and Abraham?

formChoices.sentence: The religion of Moses (pbuh) was the same as [choice] Jacob (pbuh), which was Islamic monotheism.
Moses (pbuh), therefore, was one of the [choice] of Abraham (pbuh) …
… every prophet who came after Abraham (pbuh) was one of Abraham’s [choice].

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “The same as that of Jacob” compares religion with religion (“that” replaces “the religion”), not religion with a person. “One of the + plural noun”: one of the descendants, one of Abraham’s successors. A descendant comes later in a family line; a successor follows someone in a role.

feedback.correct: Well done. You chose the forms that express sameness and continuity accurately.
feedback.incorrect: Check that “the same as …” compares two religions, that “one of” is followed by a plural noun, and which word means someone who comes after. See the end of Chapter 17.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explaining Continuity
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in five sentences how Moses is linked to Jacob and Abraham.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does Moses carry on Abraham’s message?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The task asks learners to build a connected explanation rather than list family names.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “who” or “which” once, and “Therefore” or “so”.
discussionPrompts.example: The chapter explains that Moses (pbuh) did not bring a completely new religion. His religion was the same as that of Jacob (pbuh), which was Islamic monotheism. Jacob (pbuh), who was the grandson of Abraham (pbuh), was his forefather. Therefore, Moses (pbuh) was one of the descendants of Abraham (pbuh). Every prophet after Abraham (pbuh) was one of his successors, so Moses (pbuh) continues the same line.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: According to the verse, what has the Pharaoh done?
options: He has built a new city.
He has gone beyond all limits.
beforeYouRead.quote: He has gone beyond all limits

iCan: I can explain how Moses (pbuh) is linked to Jacob and Abraham (pbuh).
I can add extra information about a person with “who” or “which”.
I can explain a line of continuity in five clear sentences.

pages.title: Moses and Aaron
pages.content: Moses (pbuh) was not alone in this very hard task. Aaron (pbuh), who was the brother of Moses and the prophet sent to the Children of Israel, helped Moses (pbuh). They went together to the Pharaoh and delivered the message. Moses (pbuh) told him about Allah, the duties of monotheism and worship of Allah, as well as His mercy and His Paradise. The Pharaoh listened to Moses’ speech, and he thought that Moses had lost his mind. He asked, “What do you want?” Moses (pbuh) answered, “I want you to send the Children of Israel with me.” Moses (pbuh) asked the Pharaoh for permission to take the Israelites into the desert to sacrifice according to the religion of his ancestors. The Pharaoh asked, “Why should I send them, as they are my slaves?” Moses (pbuh) replied, “Their Lord is Allah.” The Pharaoh asked Moses (pbuh) where he had found the courage to worship Allah. Didn’t he know that the Pharaoh was a god? Then the Pharaoh mockingly asked whether his name was Moses. Moses (pbuh) said, “Yes.” “Are you not that Moses who we took from the Nile as a defenseless baby?” asked the Pharaoh. “Aren’t you that Moses who we raised in our palace, who ate our food, upon whom our charity and wealth were showered?”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:moses-nile
__historical_entity__:moses-pharaohs-palace
__historical_entity__:moses-pharaoh
__historical_entity__:moses-children-of-israel
To pass on a message or news to the person it is meant for.
Kindness and help given to people in need.
The act of allowing someone to do something.
Unable to protect yourself.
In a way that laughs at someone and shows no respect.

hotspots.title: Two Brothers, One Message
hotspots.description: Aaron (pbuh), a prophet himself, went with his brother Moses (pbuh) to take Allah’s message to the Pharaoh.

hotspots.title: “They Are My Slaves”
hotspots.description: The Pharaoh refused to free the Israelites, calling them his slaves, but Moses (pbuh) answered that their Lord was Allah.

exercises.title: Whose Slaves?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 18 supports.
exercises.question: Moses tells the Pharaoh, “Their Lord is Allah.” Which claim of the Pharaoh is he rejecting?
options: that Moses had lost his mind
that the Children of Israel were his slaves
that Moses had been taken from the Nile as a baby
that the Israelites should sacrifice in the desert
exercises.explanation: The Pharaoh asks, “Why should I send them, as they are my slaves?” Moses replies, “Their Lord is Allah.” His answer denies that the Pharaoh owns them: They belong to Allah.

feedback.correct: Yes. Moses answers the Pharaoh’s claim of ownership: The Israelites’ Lord is Allah, not the Pharaoh.
feedback.incorrect: Read the Pharaoh’s question just before “Their Lord is Allah.” in the middle of Chapter 18.

languageFocusExercises.title: Questions as Power Moves
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each question from Chapter 18 with what it does in the dialogue.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does each question do in the dialogue?

matchingPairs.left: “What do you want?”
matchingPairs.right: demands that Moses state his request directly

matchingPairs.left: “Why should I send them, as they are my slaves?”
matchingPairs.right: rejects the request through a claim of ownership

matchingPairs.left: Didn’t he know that the Pharaoh was a god?
matchingPairs.right: presents Pharaoh’s claim as something everyone should already accept

matchingPairs.left: “Are you not that Moses who we took from the Nile as a defenseless baby?”
matchingPairs.right: uses Moses’ past and upbringing to put pressure on him

correctAnswer.“What do you want?”: demands that Moses state his request directly
correctAnswer.“Why should I send them, as they are my: rejects the request through a claim of ownership
correctAnswer.Didn’t he know that the Pharaoh was a go: presents Pharaoh’s claim as something everyone should already accept

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The questions are not neutral requests for information. A negative question (“Didn’t he know …?”, “Are you not …?”) expects agreement and puts pressure on the listener; “Why should I …?” is a rhetorical refusal.

feedback.correct: Correct. You identified what each question does, not only what it asks.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what answer each speaker expects. Which question refuses, which demands, and which ones expect “yes”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Reported and Direct Questions
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you change reported words into direct words, and back?

transformItems.source: Then the Pharaoh mockingly asked whether his name was Moses.
transformItems.frame: Then the Pharaoh asked mockingly, “[blank] Moses?”

transformItems.source: The Pharaoh asked Moses (pbuh) where he had found the courage to worship Allah.
transformItems.frame: The Pharaoh asked Moses, “Where [blank] the courage to worship Allah?”

transformItems.source: Moses (pbuh) answered, “I want you to send the Children of Israel with me.”
transformItems.frame: Moses (pbuh) answered that he [blank] the Pharaoh to send the Children of Israel with him.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses “whether/if” and statement word order; the direct question inverts (“Is your name …?”). “Where he had found” becomes “Where did you find / have you found …?”. When reporting, present “want” moves back to “wanted”, and “me” becomes “him”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved accurately between reported and direct speech.
feedback.incorrect: Direct questions need question word order (“Is your name …?”, “Where did you …?”). Reported statements move the tense back. Check Chapter 18.

languageFocusExercises.title: Ownership vs Lordship
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the contrast that the dialogue itself builds.
languageFocusExercises.question: What difference does the dialogue itself show?
options: Both speakers agree that Pharaoh owns every person absolutely.
Moses asks Pharaoh to become the Lord of the Israelites.
Pharaoh calls the Israelites his slaves, while Moses states that their Lord is Allah.
Pharaoh calls the Israelites his guests, while Moses calls them his servants.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The possessives carry the argument: “my slaves” (Pharaoh’s claim of human ownership) against “Their Lord is Allah” (Moses’ statement of divine lordship).

feedback.correct: Correct. The possessives “my slaves” and “their Lord” carry the contrast.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the Pharaoh’s question about sending the Israelites and at Moses’ short reply.

languageFocusExercises.title: Two Questions, Two Aims
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose two questions from the chapter. Explain in 5–6 sentences what each one does.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the Pharaoh use questions to control the talk?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: B2 analysis should identify what questions do rhetorically, not only what information they contain.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Compare the two questions with “whereas” or “while”.
discussionPrompts.example: The Pharaoh’s first question, “What do you want?”, looks simple, but it makes Moses (pbuh) explain himself. His second question, “Why should I send them, as they are my slaves?”, already contains his answer. Whereas the first question asks for information, the second claims ownership of the people. In this way, the Pharaoh tries to move the talk from the message to his own power. Moses (pbuh) answers, “Their Lord is Allah,” and turns the dialogue back to lordship.

pages.title: Pharaoh’s Threat
pages.content: “Are you not that Moses who was the murderer of an Egyptian man? Killing is an act of unbelief. So, when you killed, you were not a believer. You are on the run from the law, and now you are here to talk to me!” Moses (pbuh) knew that Pharaoh’s talk about his past, his upbringing, and the Pharaoh’s charity was his way of threatening him. Ignoring his irony, Moses (pbuh) explained that he was not a disbeliever when he killed the Egyptian; rather, he had committed the act only by accident. He explained to the Pharaoh that, despite the fact that the killing was an accident, he had left Egypt out of fear of revenge. He told him that Allah had forgiven him and made him one of His Messengers. In the Pharaoh’s land, it was not permitted to worship anyone other than the Pharaoh himself. After long dialogues, Moses (pbuh) understood that the intellectual discussions did not work. The Pharaoh finally started openly threatening Moses (pbuh). He said, “If you accept any god other than me, I will imprison you!” Moses (pbuh) said, “What if I bring you something convincing and true?” He had no choice but to display the miracles. The Pharaoh said, “Bring it if you are honest!”

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the parts of Chapter 19: the Pharaoh’s own words, or Moses’ answer as reported?

pages.title: The Contest Begins
pages.content: So, when Moses (pbuh) threw his staff, it clearly turned into a snake. And when he pulled out his hand, everyone could see that it was white (Surah ash-Shu’ara: 30-33). It was a hand that shed light! Pharaoh’s eyes were dazzled by the brightness of the hand. These two miracles by Prophet Moses (pbuh) actually demonstrated his prophethood. The Pharaoh spoke to his advisors out of fear that his rule was in danger. His advisors recommended that the Pharaoh detain Moses (pbuh) and call upon the cleverest magicians. They might demonstrate their magic abilities and transform sticks into snakes. In this way, they aimed to lessen the impact of Moses’ miracles on the population. It was decided that a contest would be held between the magicians of Egypt and Moses (pbuh). The aim was to defeat Moses (pbuh) and make him fail in his claim. But things did not go as the Pharaoh had expected. Then the crowd gathered. Everyone was eager to watch this fantastic competition. The magicians wanted to prove that Moses (pbuh) was a liar and a cheat. Moses (pbuh) requested a performance by the magicians first. They threw their magical objects on the floor, and their staffs and ropes took the shapes of moving snakes. However, this was only an illusion.

pages.title: The Magicians Believe
pages.content: But this illusion, performed with great skill, even filled Moses’ heart with fear for a moment, and the Pharaoh and his soldiers gave a loud cheer. Moses (pbuh) then threw his staff. His stick started to twist and grew into a huge snake. Moses’ snake ate all the magicians’ fake snakes, and the Pharaoh and his men watched in silence. When Moses (pbuh) reached down to take it, it transformed into a staff again. After seeing Moses’ power, the magicians bowed down to Allah and said, “We believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron.” At that time, magicians were not merely performers, but the elite intellectual scholars of ancient Egypt. So it was a major defeat and disappointment for the Pharaoh. When he faced the miracles, the Pharaoh was utterly horrified. He then called for all his ministers and men in positions of responsibility. The prime minister asked, “Will we leave Moses and his people to corrupt and manipulate the rest of the people on earth so that they leave your worship?” Upon this, the Pharaoh announced commands, and his men began to kill the sons and imprison others. Moses (pbuh) couldn’t do anything but advise his people to be patient. Moses (pbuh) made the same request that Pharaoh free the Children of Israel from slavery. The Pharaoh replied by ordering all his subjects, including the Children of Israel, to attend a large assembly and reminding them that he was their master and met all of their needs. They lacked vision since they had been under oppression for a long time. They believed that their king was wealthy and could meet all of their material needs. They ignored Moses’ (pbuh) call and unquestioningly obeyed the Pharaoh.

languageFocusExercises.title: Why “not merely … but …” Matters
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 21 and choose what the contrast adds.

options: It says the magicians had no real knowledge or skill.
It explains why the magicians’ belief carried intellectual and political weight.

It shows that the magicians performed only for entertainment.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not merely A, but B” rejects a smaller description (performers) and replaces it with a larger one (elite scholars). This explains the next sentence: “So it was a major defeat …” — the experts’ recognition damaged Pharaoh’s position.
