pages.title: The Red Sea Opens
pages.content:
The Pharaoh became ruder and more arrogant. He declared to his people, “Pharaoh is the only god.” It seemed that the Pharaoh would never accept Moses’ (pbuh) teachings or put an end to the hard days of the Children of Israel.
Upon this, the Pharaoh began to take even harsher steps. Allah commanded Moses (pbuh) to leave. This later became known as the Exodus. To escape Pharaoh’s genocide, Moses (pbuh) and the Children of Israel, finding no other way, set out at night. In the darkness of the night and under Moses’ (pbuh) guidance the Children of Israel journeyed toward the Red Sea.
When the sun rose, they reached the beach. The Pharaoh realized their departure, so he mobilized his huge army and started following them. Soon, they easily managed to catch up with them. The Israelites panicked. They were trapped with the Red Sea in front and the king’s army behind them. However, Moses (pbuh) said that Allah was with them and would show them the way to safety (see Surah ash-Shu’ara: 61-62). Allah told Moses (pbuh), “Hit the sea with your staff!” Moses did it. Then a strong wind blew, the sun shone brightly, and immediately the sea parted; the waves stood like mountains on each side. The Children of Israel passed through this dry land and were saved. Allah narrated: “And We inspired Moses, saying: ‘Take away My servants by night; verily, you will be pursued.’
Then Pharaoh sent callers to all the cities, saying: ‘Truly! These indeed are but a small band. And verily, they are angering us; but we are an alert crowd.’ So We removed them from gardens and springs, treasures, and every kind of honorable place. Thus, We turned Pharaoh’s people out, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them. So they pursued them at sunrise. And when the two groups saw each other, the people of Moses said: ‘We are sure to be caught up with.’ Moses said: ‘Truly! With me is my Lord; He will guide me.’”

languageFocusExercises.title: Two Responses to the Same Danger
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the lines from Chapter 22: fear of what they see, or trust in Allah?
languageFocusExercises.question: Who panics, and who trusts?

items: The Israelites panicked.
The Children of Israel were trapped with the Red Sea in front and the king’s army behind them.
‘We are sure to be caught up with.’

items: Moses (pbuh) said that Allah was with them and would show them the way to safety

Fear of the visible danger: The Children of Israel were trapped with the Red Sea in front and the king’s army behind them.
‘We are sure to be caught up with.’

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Both groups speak with certainty, but about different things: “We are sure to be caught up with” is certain about the danger; “He will guide me” is certain about guidance. In the narrative, “However” marks the turn from panic to trust, and the reported “would show” looks forward to a way that is not yet visible.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated certainty about danger from certainty about guidance.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each line is sure about: Being caught, or being guided? Check the end of Chapter 22 and the Qur’anic lines that close it.

languageFocusExercises.title: Two Ways to Tell the Escape

languageFocusExercises.title: Catching Up and Parting
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each sentence from Chapter 22.

formChoices.sentence: Soon, they easily managed [choice] up with them.
Then a strong wind blew, the sun shone brightly, and immediately the sea [choice]; the waves stood like mountains on each side.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Manage + to-infinitive” shows success in a difficult action. “Part” can be intransitive: “the sea parted” describes a completed event in the past simple, in line with the other verbs in the sentence (blew, shone, stood).

feedback.correct: Well done. You chose the right pattern after “manage” and the right past form.
feedback.incorrect: Which form follows “manage”? And which tense do the other verbs in the long sentence use? Check Chapter 22.

languageFocusExercises.title: Trust Before Seeing
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in 6–8 sentences how the people’s fear differs from Moses’ trust.
languageFocusExercises.question: What could the people see, and what did Moses say?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: B2 analysis distinguishes present evidence, stated confidence, and later outcome instead of collapsing them into one moment.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Keep apart what they see, what Moses says, and what happens later.
discussionPrompts.example: When the sun rose, the Israelites could see the Red Sea in front of them and the king’s army behind them. From what they could see, there was no way out, so they panicked. Moses (pbuh), however, said that Allah was with them and would show them the way to safety. At that moment, nothing visible supported his words. Only afterwards did Allah tell him to hit the sea with his staff. Then the sea parted, and the Children of Israel passed through on dry land. So his confidence came before the evidence, not after it.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How did the Israelites feel when they saw the army behind them?
beforeYouRead.quote: The Israelites panicked.

iCan: I can tell how the Children of Israel escaped through the Red Sea.
I can join two actions in one sentence with an -ing phrase.
I can keep apart what people saw, what was said and what happened next.

pages.title: Pharaoh Drowns
pages.content: “Then We inspired Moses, saying: ‘Strike the sea with your stick.’ And it parted, and each separate part of that sea water became like the huge, firm mass of a mountain. Then We brought near the others (Pharaoh’s party) to that place. And We saved Moses and all those with him. Then We drowned the others. Verily! In this is indeed a sign (or a proof), yet most of them are not believers. And verily, your Lord! He is truly the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.” (Surah ash-Shu’ara: 52-68) The Pharaoh and his army saw the miracle. But the Pharaoh turned to his men and said, “Look! The sea has opened at my command.” He and his soldiers saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power. They entered the parted waters, and when they were midway, Allah commanded the sea to return to its former state. The sea closed over them, and they drowned. Moses (pbuh) led the Children of Israel toward the land of Canaan. (The land of Canaan: the land of Palestine. It is the historical homeland where Jacob’s (pbuh) offspring settled.) On the way, they saw a group of people that worshipped idols and calves.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:moses-canaan
__historical_entity__:moses-pharaoh
__historical_entity__:moses-children-of-israel
Very unusual and surprising; far beyond what is normal.
To put guidance or an idea directly into someone’s heart and mind.
To die, or to make someone die, under water.
At the middle point between the start and the end.
Statues or images that people worship as gods.
The country or land where a people comes from.

hotspots.title: The Pharaoh’s False Claim
hotspots.description: The Pharaoh told his men that the sea had opened at his own command.

hotspots.title: The Sea Closes
hotspots.description: When the Pharaoh and his soldiers were halfway across, the sea returned and drowned them.

exercises.title: The Pharaoh’s Last Claim
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 23.
exercises.question: When the Pharaoh saw the sea open, he accepted that it was a sign from Allah.
exercises.explanation: The Pharaoh told his men, “Look! The sea has opened at my command.” He and his soldiers “saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power.” They entered the parted waters, and the sea closed over them.

feedback.correct: Correct. Even in front of the miracle, the Pharaoh claimed the power for himself.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 23, after the Qur’anic passage. What did the Pharaoh say to his men?

languageFocusExercises.title: Event vs Self-Serving Interpretation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the parts of Chapter 23: what happened, or the Pharaoh’s explanation?
languageFocusExercises.question: What really happened, and what did the Pharaoh claim?

items: The Pharaoh and his army saw the miracle.
Allah commanded the sea to return to its former state.
The sea closed over them, and they drowned.
“Look! The sea has opened at my command.”
saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power

What the narrator reports: The Pharaoh and his army saw the miracle.
Allah commanded the sea to return to its former state.
The sea closed over them, and they drowned.
The Pharaoh’s interpretation: “Look! The sea has opened at my command.”
saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The narrator names the event “the miracle” and gives its cause (“Allah commanded …”). The Pharaoh’s words and “saw … as a sign of …” present his interpretation. “See X as Y” reports how someone interprets something, not what is true.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the narrated events from the Pharaoh’s claim.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who is speaking or interpreting. “Saw … as …” and the Pharaoh’s quotation show his view; the narrator reports the cause and the outcome.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reporting a Claim
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say the Pharaoh’s words and what his men believed?

transformItems.source: But the Pharaoh turned to his men and said, “Look! The sea has opened at my command.”
transformItems.frame: But the Pharaoh told his men that the sea [blank] at his command.

transformItems.source: He and his soldiers saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power.
transformItems.frame: He and his soldiers believed that this extraordinary event [blank] Pharaoh’s godlike power.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: When a claim is reported after a past verb, the present perfect moves back to the past perfect (“has opened” → “had opened”). “Saw X as a sign of Y” can be rephrased with “believed that X showed Y”; both keep it clear that this is their belief, not the narrator’s explanation.

feedback.correct: Well done. You reported the claim and kept it as the Pharaoh’s view.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: move “has opened” one step back. Item 2: what did they believe the event was a sign of? Check the middle of Chapter 23.

languageFocusExercises.title: Whose Explanation?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in 5–7 sentences why the Pharaoh says the sea opened at his command.
languageFocusExercises.question: Who really opened the sea, and why does the Pharaoh claim it?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The task requires B2 evidence-versus-interpretation reasoning grounded in the source.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Quote or retell two things from the chapter that show the real cause.
discussionPrompts.example: The Pharaoh told his men, “Look! The sea has opened at my command.” The chapter, however, gives a different cause: Allah inspired Moses (pbuh) to strike the sea with his stick, and it parted. The Pharaoh saw this extraordinary event as a sign of his own godlike power. This explanation helped him to keep control over his soldiers. The ending shows that it was false: when they were midway, Allah commanded the sea to return to its former state. So the chapter presents his words as a claim, not as the explanation.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Where did Moses (pbuh) lead the Children of Israel next?
beforeYouRead.quote: Moses (pbuh) led the Children of Israel toward the land of Canaan.

iCan: I can tell what happened to the Pharaoh and his army.
I can report how someone explained an event.
I can show why an explanation serves the person who gives it.

pages.title: The Calf and the Torah
pages.content: Some of them said, “O Moses! Make something like that for us so we can worship it!” Moses (pbuh) patiently advised them, “Allah saved you from the Pharaoh’s oppression. The Egyptians were killing your sons and using your daughters as servants. Despite this, will you rebel against Allah and fall into idol worship?!” When Moses (pbuh) led the Children of Israel out of Egypt, he told his people that he would bring them a Book from Allah. Allah told Moses (pbuh) to go up Mount Tur. Moses (pbuh) left his brother Aaron (pbuh) in charge and went up Mount Tur himself. He stayed on Mount Tur for forty days and worshipped Allah (see Surah al-A’raf: 142). He heard the words of Allah directly. During this time, the Torah was given to him by Allah. Moses (pbuh) returned to his people with the Torah, but unfortunately saw his people singing and dancing around the calf statue. He was deeply disappointed. His story would not end here. He would face many difficult tests to guide the Children of Israel to the truth, but they continued disobeying. Moses’ (pbuh) efforts to guide them to the right path are the reason he is known as the Prophet of Great Determination.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:moses-egypt-ancient
__historical_entity__:moses-mount-sinai
__historical_entity__:moses-pharaoh
__historical_entity__:moses-children-of-israel
__historical_entity__:moses-ancient-egyptians
Cruel and unfair treatment of people by those in power.
To refuse to do what someone in authority tells you.
A young cow; here, a statue of one that people worshipped.
The quality of continuing to try even when something is difficult.
Calmly, without getting angry or giving up.

hotspots.title: Forty Days on Mount Tur
hotspots.description: Moses (pbuh) stayed on the mountain for forty days, heard Allah’s words and received the Torah.

hotspots.title: Dancing Around the Calf
hotspots.description: Moses (pbuh) returned to find his people singing and dancing around a calf statue.

exercises.title: Great Determination
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that Chapter 24 supports.
exercises.question: According to the writer, why is Moses known as the Prophet of Great Determination?
options: because he stayed on Mount Tur for forty days
because of his efforts to guide his people to the right path
because he received the Torah from Allah
because he defeated the magicians of Egypt
exercises.explanation: The last sentence says: “Moses’ (pbuh) efforts to guide them to the right path are the reason he is known as the Prophet of Great Determination.” Even after he saw his people “singing and dancing around the calf statue,” he kept trying to guide them.

feedback.correct: Yes. His determination shows in his long, patient efforts to guide a people who kept disobeying.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 24. The writer states the reason there.

languageFocusExercises.title: Looking Forward from the Ending
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the end of Chapter 24 and choose what “would” does.
languageFocusExercises.question: “His story would not end here. He would face many difficult tests …” What does “would” do here?
options: It describes something Moses used to do regularly.
It describes an imagined situation that never happened.
It looks forward from a point in the past to what was still to come.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Would” here is the future in the past: from the moment he returns with the Torah, the narrator looks ahead to later events. It tells the reader that liberation is not the end of the story.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Would” looks ahead from a past moment in the story.
feedback.incorrect: Are these tests a past habit, a wish, or events that came later than the moment described? Read the last lines of Chapter 24.

languageFocusExercises.title: Promise and Gift
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say his promise and “was given … by Allah”?

transformItems.source: When Moses (pbuh) led the Children of Israel out of Egypt, he told his people that he would bring them a Book from Allah.
transformItems.frame: When Moses (pbuh) led the Children of Israel out of Egypt, he told his people, “I [blank] you a Book from Allah.”

transformItems.source: During this time, the Torah was given to him by Allah.
transformItems.frame: During this time, Allah [blank] the Torah.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Reported “would bring” goes back to “will bring” in direct speech, and “them” becomes “you”. The passive “was given to him by Allah” focuses on the Torah; the active “Allah gave him the Torah” focuses on the giver.

feedback.correct: Well done. You rebuilt the promise and the active sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: in direct speech, “would” becomes “will”. Item 2: the active of “was given to him” is “gave him”. Check Chapter 24.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the verb after “efforts”, and the verb after “saw his people”?

errorItems.sentence: Moses’s (pbuh) efforts to guide them to the right path is the reason he is known as the Prophet of Great Determination.
Moses (pbuh) returned to his people with the Torah, but unfortunately saw his people to sing and dancing around the calf statue.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The subject is “efforts” (plural), so the verb is “are”, even though a singular noun (“path”) comes just before it. “See + person + -ing” describes an action in progress that someone witnesses: “saw his people singing and dancing”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the agreement and the pattern after “saw his people”.
feedback.incorrect: Find the real subject of the first sentence. In the second, both verbs after “saw his people” should have the same form. Check the end of Chapter 24.

languageFocusExercises.title: Liberation Is Not the End
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Explain in 7–8 sentences why freedom is not the end of the story.
languageFocusExercises.question: What new duties come after freedom?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A B2 synthesis should connect rescue, guidance, disobedience, and continuing determination without reducing the ending to one event.

feedback.correct: Check that each target form does a clear job in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Look back at how the chapter uses these forms, then revise your paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “Despite …”, “would” for what came later, and two facts from the chapter.
discussionPrompts.example: The final chapter shows that leaving Egypt was not the end of the story. Despite being saved from the Pharaoh, some of the people asked Moses (pbuh) to make them something to worship. He reminded them that Allah had saved them from oppression. He had also told them that he would bring them a Book from Allah. While he stayed on Mount Tur for forty days, the Torah was given to him. However, when he returned, he saw his people singing and dancing around the calf statue. The text says that his story would not end here and that he would face many difficult tests. So freedom brought a continuing responsibility: To stay on the right path.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What were his people doing when Moses (pbuh) returned?
options: singing and dancing around the calf statue
beforeYouRead.quote: saw his people singing and dancing around the calf statue

iCan: I can tell what happened after the escape from Egypt.
I can talk about the future as it was seen from the past.
I can explain why freedom brings new responsibility.

groupTask.title: Evidence or Interpretation? A Class Exhibition

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You copy three sentences from your two chapters exactly as they are written.

roles.name: Source Checker
roles.job: You decide for each sentence: Does the book state it, does it come from sources or a character, or is it an interpretation?

roles.name: Writer
roles.job: You write the analysis using at least three patterns from the Language Focus pages.

roles.name: Designer and Presenter
roles.job: You lay out the poster or record the two-minute audio report and present it.

steps: Choose one chapter pair: Chapters 1–2, 18–19 or 22–23.
Copy at least three sentences exactly, for example: “So the pharaoh who drowned at sea was probably Ramses II.” or “Look! The sea has opened at my command.”

Sort your sentences into three columns: What the book states, what it attributes to sources or characters, and what is interpretation. Use patterns such as “according to”, “probably”, “saw … as …”, “rather” and “not merely … but …”.
End with one lesson for reading news or social media today. Nobody speaks as a person from the story; you only report and analyse what the book says.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its poster or plays its audio report, reads one exact quote aloud and explains which column it belongs in.
groupTask.solo: Choose one chapter pair, copy three exact sentences, sort them into the three columns and write a short paragraph ending with one lesson for reading the news.

legend.route:exodus: The Exodus to the Red Sea

places.name: Egypt
places.text: Around 1700 BC, in the time of Prophet Joseph (pbuh), the Israelites settled in Egypt. Later, the pharaohs made them work on huge projects, such as the new capital city of Ramses. In the Nile Delta, canals were built for irrigation, transportation and trade. Moses (pbuh) was raised as a prince in the Pharaoh’s palace.
places.teacherNote: All dates in the B2 text are approximate, and the text itself says that the exact date of the Exodus is unknown. The text does not say where the palace or the capital city of Ramses was, so Egypt is shown as a region.
places.question: Why did the pharaohs need so many workers?

places.name: The Nile
places.text: “Egypt is the gift of the Nile,” said the historian Herodotus: The fertile waters of the river were the source of life for Egypt. Moses’ mother put her baby into a basket on the waters of the Nile. The river carried him to the Pharaoh’s palace, where he was given the name “Musa”.
places.teacherNote: The text does not say where on the Nile the basket was found. The soft area only shows the river in Egypt. Chapter 4 explains the name: “mu” means water and “sa” means tree in the Coptic language.
places.question: Why was control of the Nile so important for the pharaohs?

places.name: Midian
places.text: Moses (pbuh) hurried out of Egypt and crossed the hot desert, traveling by night and hiding during the day. Midian was the closest inhabited area between Egypt and Syria, in the eastern part of the Gulf of Aqaba. At a well, he helped the two daughters of Prophet Shu’ayb (pbuh). He then worked as a shepherd there for ten long years.
places.teacherNote: The text calls the water “a watering hole outside Midian” (ch. 11), “a well in Midian” (ch. 12) and “the spring” (ch. 13). Its exact place is not known.
places.question: Why were the ten years in Midian important for Moses?

places.name: Sinai
places.text: Moses left Midian with his family to return to Egypt across the Sinai. On a winter night, they reached Mount Sinai, also known as Mount Tur. There, in the sacred valley of Tuwa, Allah called Moses and gave him two signs. Later, after leading his people out of Egypt, Moses stayed on Mount Tur for forty days, and the Torah was given to him.
places.teacherNote: The soft area shows the region, not an exact peak or valley: The text does not say where Mount Tur or Tuwa is. It also does not say directly that the Mount Tur of chapter 24 is the same place as in chapter 15, but chapter 15 says Mount Sinai is also known as Mount Tur.
places.question: What did Allah tell Moses to take off in the sacred valley?

places.name: The Red Sea
places.text: The Children of Israel set out at night and journeyed toward the Red Sea. When the sun rose, they reached the beach, with the sea in front of them and the Pharaoh’s army behind. A strong wind blew, the sea parted, and the waves stood like mountains on each side. The Pharaoh and his army entered the parted waters and drowned.
places.teacherNote: The exact place of the crossing is not known; the soft area at the Gulf of Suez is approximate. Chapter 2 says the pharaoh who drowned was probably Ramses II and that most sources place the Exodus in the early 13th century BC, but its exact date is unknown.
places.question: How did the Pharaoh explain the parting of the sea to his men?

places.name: The Land of Canaan
places.text: After the sea crossing, Moses (pbuh) led the Children of Israel toward the land of Canaan, the land of Palestine. It is the historical homeland where Jacob’s (pbuh) offspring settled. On the way, they saw a group of people who worshipped idols and calves.
places.teacherNote: The text gives no route and no place for the people who worshipped idols. The line on the map only shows the direction, “toward the land of Canaan”.
places.question: What did some of the Children of Israel ask Moses on the way?

challenge.prompt: Find Egypt. The Israelites settled here in the time of Prophet Joseph (pbuh).
Find Midian. It was in the eastern part of the Gulf of Aqaba.
Find Sinai. Moses crossed it on his way from Midian back to Egypt.
Find the Red Sea. The Children of Israel set out at night and reached its beach at sunrise.
Find the land of Canaan. Moses led his people toward it after the sea crossing.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Review the narrative themes, miracles, and historical lessons of Moses (pbuh).

exercises.title: What the Name Records
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 4, what does the name “Musa” record about the baby?
options: That he came from a noble Egyptian family.
Where he was found: in the water, at a tree.
That he would one day lead the Israelites.
That Queen Asiye had chosen the name herself.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “The child at the foot of the tree in the waters of the Nile was given the name “Musa” in the Pharaoh’s palace. It was a combination of the words “mu” meaning water, and “sa” meaning tree in the Coptic language.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. In Coptic “mu” means water and “sa” means tree, so the name keeps the place where the baby was found.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the middle of Chapter 4, where the writer explains the two Coptic words inside the name.

exercises.title: The Nurse’s Answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer according to the story.
exercises.question: The Pharaoh asked the nurse, “Who are you?” According to Chapter 8, what made her calm answer possible?
options: Queen Asiye had told her what to say.
The Pharaoh already knew who she really was.
Moses’ sister answered the question for her.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “Allah gave her inner strength, and she answered, “I have sweet milk and a sweet scent, so no baby refuses me.” This answer pleased the Pharaoh.”

feedback.correct: Right. The mother could not reveal who she was, and the story says it was Allah who gave her the strength to answer calmly.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first lines of Chapter 8. What does the writer say happened just before she answered the Pharaoh?

exercises.title: Before the Mission
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: Even before he became a prophet, the weak and oppressed turned to young Moses because of the gifts Allah had given him.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “He had not yet been given the prophetic mission.” … “Allah gave Moses perfect health, strength, wisdom, and knowledge. Because of these gifts, the weak and oppressed always looked to him for protection and justice.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. Health, strength, wisdom and knowledge made him the person the oppressed looked to for protection and justice.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the second half of Chapter 8. What gifts did Allah give Moses, and who looked to him because of them?

exercises.title: A Word in Context
exercises.instructions: Choose the meaning that fits the context.
exercises.question: In Chapter 10 Moses says, “Verily, you are a plain troublemaker!” What does “plain” mean here?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “The very next day, Moses saw the same Israelite involved in another dispute. Moses understood that the Israelite was a quarrelsome man.” Chapter 10: “Moses said to him: “Verily, you are a plain troublemaker!””

feedback.correct: Exactly. “Plain” means clear to everyone: After a second fight in two days, the man’s troublemaking was obvious.
feedback.incorrect: Compare Chapter 10 with the end of Chapter 9. What had Moses just seen the man do again, and how clear was it?

exercises.title: A Safe Land
exercises.instructions: Connect the two chapters and decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: Shu’ayb’s words in Chapter 14, “you have escaped from the wrongdoers,” agree with how Chapter 11 describes Midian.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “He headed for the land of Midian, which was the closest inhabited area between Egypt and Syria. It was a region not ruled by the Pharaoh.” Chapter 14: “The old man comforted him, “Do not fear, you have escaped from the wrongdoers.””

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. Midian was outside the Pharaoh’s rule, so Shu’ayb could tell Moses that he was safe there.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the middle of Chapter 11: who ruled Midian? Then compare it with Shu’ayb’s first words in Chapter 14.

exercises.title: A Word in Context
exercises.instructions: Choose the meaning that fits the context.
exercises.question: In Chapter 12 we read, “The bottoms of his feet were raw.” What does “raw” mean here?
options: cold after the nights in the desert
bare because he had lost his sandals
sore and damaged from long walking
wet from the water at the well
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “The bottoms of his feet were raw. They were worn out from hard walking on sand and rocks and from the dust. He urgently needed a new pair of sandals, food and drink.”

feedback.correct: Right. The next sentence explains it: His feet were worn out from walking on sand and rocks, so they were sore and damaged.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence that follows “raw” in Chapter 12. What had happened to his feet on the journey?

exercises.title: The Fire at Night
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer according to the story.
exercises.question: Why did Moses approach the fire at Mount Sinai?
options: He wanted to ask the Pharaoh’s men for help.
He had heard a voice and went to find the caller.
He had lost his way and hoped for warmth and a guide.
He wanted to offer a sacrifice like his ancestors.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 15: “There, Moses discovered that he had lost his way.” … “Moses noticed a fire in the distance and approached it, hoping to bring his family some fire to warm themselves and find a guide by the fire.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. It was a cold winter night and he had lost his way, so he hoped for fire for his family and someone to guide them. The voice came only as he neared the fire.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the start of Chapter 15. What problem did Moses have on the way, and when did he hear the voice: Before or after he approached the fire?

exercises.title: On Mount Tur
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 24, Moses took Aaron with him up Mount Tur and came back with the Torah on the same day.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 24: “Moses (pbuh) left his brother Aaron (pbuh) in charge and went up Mount Tur himself. He stayed on Mount Tur for forty days and worshipped Allah.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. Aaron stayed behind in charge of the people, and Moses stayed on the mountain for forty days.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the middle of Chapter 24. Who stayed with the people, and how long was Moses on the mountain?

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the story in one place.

vocabulary.definition: Cruel and unfair rule by someone who has total power.
vocabulary.storyExample: Moses (pbuh) is one of the great prophets according to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, who saved the Children of Israel from Pharaoh’s despotism.

vocabulary.definition: To come from a particular person, place or source.
vocabulary.storyExample: (Pharaohs were the kings of ancient Egypt.) The Children of Israel, or the Israelites, originated from Prophet Jacob (pbuh) and were Jews by birth.

vocabulary.definition: To go to live permanently in a new place.
vocabulary.storyExample: During the time of Prophet Joseph (pbuh), around 1700 BC (BC: Before Christ), the Israelites settled in Egypt.

vocabulary.definition: The group of people in a society who hold power and govern.
vocabulary.storyExample: To prevent them from becoming a ruling class, local rulers tried to stop the population growth by making life difficult for the Children of Israel.

vocabulary.definition: The role of guiding and directing a group of people.
vocabulary.storyExample: Almost the entire Torah consists of the history of Moses (pbuh) and the Israelites under his leadership.

vocabulary.definition: A person from an earlier generation of your family; an ancestor.
vocabulary.storyExample: As Prophet Isaac (pbuh), Prophet Jacob (pbuh), and Prophet Joseph (pbuh) were their forefathers, the Israelites also believed in their superiority.

vocabulary.definition: The belief or state of being better or more important than others.
vocabulary.storyExample: As Prophet Isaac (pbuh), Prophet Jacob (pbuh), and Prophet Joseph (pbuh) were their forefathers, the Israelites also believed in their superiority.

vocabulary.definition: The period of time during which a king or queen rules.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Israelites were made to work to build the huge Seti temple during the reign of Seti I and the new capital city of Ramses during the reign of Ramses II.

vocabulary.definition: Public actions that show strong disagreement with something.
vocabulary.storyExample: Sources also say that because of the heavy work going on during this time, slaves, including the Israelites, were under a lot of pressure, and this pressure led to trouble and even some protests.

vocabulary.definition: Situations in which people stop obeying the authorities and violence breaks out; unrest.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the source-framing, stance, cause, contrast, condition, focus and discourse patterns developed across all twenty-four chapters.

exercises.title: Notice: Whose Claim, and How Sure?
exercises.instructions: Put each sentence from the book in the right group.
exercises.question: Is it a source, a careful guess, or a character’s view?

items: According to the sources, Seti I … was the pharaoh who oppressed the Israelites.
Ibn Abbas said, “The Pharaoh saw a fire in his vision. …”

dragDropGroups.group: The writer hedges: likely or possible, not proved
items: So the pharaoh who drowned at sea was probably Ramses II.
It is possible that some people of that period did not practise or believe in paganism.

dragDropGroups.group: A character’s view, not the writer’s
items: The Pharaoh listened to Moses’ speech, and he thought that Moses had lost his mind.
He and his soldiers saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power.

The writer reports a source: According to the sources, Seti I … was the pharaoh who oppressed the Israelites.
Ibn Abbas said, “The Pharaoh saw a fire in his vision. …”
The writer hedges: likely or possible, n: So the pharaoh who drowned at sea was probably Ramses II.
It is possible that some people of that period did not practise or believe in paganism.
A character’s view, not the writer’s: The Pharaoh listened to Moses’ speech, and he thought that Moses had lost his mind.
He and his soldiers saw this extraordinary event as a sign of Pharaoh’s godlike power.

exercises.explanation: The book separates three layers. Attribution (“according to the sources”, “Ibn Abbas said”) tells you whose information it is. Hedging (“probably”, “It is possible that …”) is the writer’s own careful judgement: likely or possible, not proved. Verbs such as “thought that …” and “saw X as Y” report how a character interprets events; they do not tell you that the interpretation is true. A B2 summary keeps each layer in place.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept sources, the writer’s hedges and the characters’ views apart.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the signal words: according to / said (a source), probably / possible (a hedge), thought / saw … as (a character’s view).

exercises.title: Notice: Not Only … / Not Merely …
exercises.instructions: Read the two sentences. Then choose the best explanation.
exercises.question: Chapter 3: “… god-king authority was based not only on the richness of the river, but also on the manpower of the slaves …” Chapter 21: “At that time, magicians were not merely performers, but the elite intellectual scholars of ancient Egypt.” What do “not only” and “not merely” do here?
options: They reject the first description as false and put a correct one in its place.
They accept the first description but show it is incomplete, then add a second, weightier point.
They show that the writer cannot decide which of the two descriptions is true.
They present the second point as a result of the first one.
exercises.explanation: ‘Not only A but also B’ and ‘not merely A, but B’ keep A (the river mattered; the magicians did perform) and add B, which carries more weight: The slaves’ manpower, the magicians’ status as scholars. Compare “rather” in Chapter 19: “he was not a disbeliever when he killed the Egyptian; rather, he had committed the act only by accident” — there the first idea is rejected completely and replaced.

feedback.correct: Correct. Both structures widen a description instead of cancelling it.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is the first part still true? Did the river matter? Did the magicians perform? Then look at what the second part adds.

exercises.title: Notice: -ing Phrases Around Moses
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences. Is the statement true or false?
exercises.question: Chapter 12: “Forgetting his thirst, Moses approached them …” Chapter 15: “… approached it, hoping to bring his family some fire …” Chapter 19: “Ignoring his irony, Moses (pbuh) explained that he was not a disbeliever …” — Statement: The -ing phrases describe actions that happen only after the main action is finished.
exercises.explanation: The -ing phrase and the main verb share one subject (Moses), and they happen at the same time: While he approaches, he forgets his thirst or hopes for fire; while he explains, he ignores the Pharaoh’s irony. The phrase adds his attitude or aim to the action without a second full clause. It does not mean “afterwards”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The -ing phrases run alongside the main action and share its subject.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who forgets, who hopes and who ignores, and when. Is it the same person, at the same moment as approached / explained?

exercises.title: Build: Cause Before a Noun, a Clause or a Sentence
exercises.instructions: Choose the right words for each sentence from the book.

formChoices.sentence: Control of the Nile River was vital. [choice], the geographical structure of the land was reshaped by human power.
[choice] the crowd at the water source, the young women could only water their animals after the male shepherds had taken their flocks away.
[choice] they needed someone reliable and strong, one of the daughters advised her father to employ Moses.

exercises.explanation: Choose the linker by what follows it. A new sentence that draws a result from the previous one starts with “For this reason,”. A noun phrase (the crowd) needs ‘due to’ or ‘because of’. A clause with its own subject and verb (they needed) needs “because”. “Despite this” and “although” would signal a contrast the book does not make.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each linker to a sentence, a noun phrase or a clause.

exercises.title: Build: Do Not Overclaim
exercises.instructions: Each sentence says more than the book. Tap the strong words, then choose the book’s words.
exercises.question: Can you make each sentence as careful as the book?

errorItems.sentence: The entire Torah consists of the history of Moses (pbuh) and the Israelites under his leadership.
All of the sources state that the Exodus … must have taken place in the early thirteenth century BC.
It was certain that the Pharaoh would never accept Moses’ (pbuh) teachings or put an end to the hard days of the Children of Israel.

exercises.explanation: Quantifiers and stance verbs set the strength of a claim. “Almost the entire” and “most of the sources” leave room for exceptions; “the entire” and “all” do not. “It seemed that …” gives an impression at that moment; ‘It was certain that …’ turns it into a fact. Rewriting a text with stronger words than the source is overclaiming.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the writer’s careful degree of certainty.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with the book: The opening of Chapter 1, the end of Chapter 2 and the start of Chapter 22. Which word leaves room for doubt or exceptions?

exercises.title: Build: Report What They Said
exercises.instructions: Report what each person said. Write only the missing words.
exercises.question: What changes when you report a question or a statement?

transformItems.source: The Pharaoh was astonished and asked, “Who are you? …”
transformItems.frame: The Pharaoh was astonished and asked her who [blank].

transformItems.source: He asked, “Why are you shepherding?”
transformItems.frame: He asked the two sisters why [blank].

transformItems.source: She said, “Our father invites you to our home so that he may thank you in person.”
transformItems.frame: She said that their father [blank] him to their home so that he might thank him in person.

exercises.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order: “Who are you?” → ‘who she was’; “Why are you shepherding?” → ‘why they were shepherding’. After a past reporting verb, present forms move back (are → were, invites → invited, may → might), and pronouns change to fit the reporter’s point of view (you → she / they / him, our → their).

feedback.correct: Correct. You moved the tense back, changed the pronouns and used statement word order.
feedback.incorrect: Check three things: Tense back (are → were), pronouns (you → she/they/him), and subject before verb in the reported question.

exercises.title: Build: A Decision Without a Named Decider
exercises.instructions: Put the parts in order to make a sentence from Chapter 20.
exercises.question: How can we give a decision without saying who made it?
exercises.explanation: “It was decided that …” is an impersonal passive: The decision is in focus and the deciders stay unnamed. Inside it, “would be held” is a passive seen from the past, looking forward to the contest. The book uses the passive in the same way elsewhere when what happens matters more than who acts: “He was placed in a basket” (Chapter 4), “the Torah was given to him by Allah” (Chapter 24).

feedback.correct: Well done. The impersonal passive puts the decision first.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the empty subject “It” and the passive verb. Then say what was decided, and between whom.

exercises.title: Use: A Report on a School Project
exercises.instructions: Complete this new text with words from the bank. Two are extra.
exercises.question: Which word fits each gap in the school report?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last term, our class started a recycling project at school. [blank] our survey, most students threw plastic bottles into ordinary bins. [blank] a lack of recycling boxes in the corridors, many bottles ended up in the rubbish. We placed new boxes on every floor, and the project helped not only the environment [blank] the school budget. The number of bottles in the ordinary bins fell by half, so the new boxes were [blank] the main reason for the change. However, we cannot be sure: Some students were also away on a school trip that month.
exercises.explanation: “According to our survey” attributes the evidence. “Due to” + a noun phrase gives the cause. “Not only … but also …” adds a second benefit. “Probably” hedges the conclusion, and the last sentence explains why: Another cause is possible. “Certainly” would overclaim, and “although” needs a clause, not a noun.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your report is sourced, connected and careful.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap ask: Is this a source, a cause before a noun, the second half of “not only”, or a hedge? Read the last sentence before you choose the hedge.

exercises.title: Use: Make the Claim More Careful
exercises.instructions: These new sentences say too much. Make them more careful. Write the missing words.
exercises.question: How can you make a claim less strong?

transformItems.source: Everyone in our class hates the new timetable.
transformItems.frame: [blank] students in our class dislike the new timetable.

transformItems.source: The new bus timetable is the reason for our late arrivals.
transformItems.frame: The new bus timetable is [blank] the reason for our late arrivals.

transformItems.source: Our survey proves that students want a longer lunch break.
transformItems.frame: Our survey [blank] that students want a longer lunch break.

exercises.explanation: Careful writers limit a claim to what the evidence shows: A quantifier instead of “everyone” (many, most, some), a hedging adverb (probably, possibly), or a softer reporting verb instead of “proves” (suggests, indicates). This is the same care the book shows with “most of the sources”, “probably” and “it seemed”.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your sentences claim only what the evidence can support.
feedback.incorrect: Replace the absolute word: everyone → many/most/some; is → is probably; proves → suggests/indicates.

exercises.title: Use: A Short Argued Paragraph
exercises.instructions: Should students do one hour of helpful work each month? Write 6–8 sentences. Talk to a partner first.
exercises.question: Can you give your view and support it?
exercises.explanation: Example: “In my view, one hour of helpful work each month would probably be good for our school. According to our class survey, most students would like to help in the library or the school garden. The project would help not only the people we support but also the students themselves because they would learn responsibility. Due to busy timetables, however, some students have little free time. It is possible that a few of them will see the hour as extra work. Although this worry is understandable, the hour would be short and flexible. It is not a punishment; rather, it is a chance to be useful.”

feedback.correct: Check your paragraph: A hedged position (probably / it seems), a source (according to), a cause (because / due to), not only … but also, a concession (although), and a correction with rather.

discussionPrompts.question: Your view — “In my view, … would probably …” or “It seems that …”
discussionPrompts.example: In my view, one hour of helpful work each month would probably make our school a kinder place. It seems that students who help others also feel more at home in their community.

discussionPrompts.question: A source and a reason — “According to …, …” / “because …” / “Due to …”
discussionPrompts.example: According to our school librarian, the library needs more helpers on Friday afternoons. Many older neighbors live alone, so a short visit can make a big difference. Due to a small budget, the school garden also needs volunteers.

discussionPrompts.question: A stronger point — “… not only … but also …”
discussionPrompts.example: This hour would not only help the library and the garden but also teach students useful skills. They would learn to plan, to work in a team and to take responsibility.

discussionPrompts.question: A doubt and your answer — “Although …, …” or “It is not …; rather, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Although some students already have a lot of homework, one hour a month is a small amount of time. It is not a punishment; rather, it is a chance to learn outside the classroom.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Test your knowledge of the entire B2 story of Prophet Moses (pbuh).

exercises.title: The Nile and Petrol
exercises.instructions: Choose the best interpretation.
exercises.question: In Chapter 3 the writer compares the Nile with “today’s petrol”. What point does the comparison make?
options: Egypt sold the Nile’s water to other lands.
A vital resource needed strong central control.
The Nile was running out, like oil does today.
Egypt’s real wealth lay in oil under the river.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3 says: “Just like today’s petrol, control of the power of the Nile also needed a strong administration, a god-king authority.” It also quotes Herodotus: “Egypt is the gift of the Nile.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Like oil today, the river was power, and whoever controlled it needed a strong state.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 3. What did control of the Nile need?

exercises.title: Saved Through Water
exercises.instructions: Choose the link the writer draws.
exercises.question: At the end of Chapter 4 the writer connects the start of Moses’ life with the end of the Pharaoh’s rule. What links them?
options: Both take place near the Pharaoh’s palace.
Both happen during the reign of Seti I.
Both are recorded only in the Torah.
Both times, rescue comes through water.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 says: “The journey of baby Moses began in the waters of the Nile. The river carried him to the Pharaoh’s palace. The salvation of Prophet Moses (pbuh) and his people from the Pharaoh also took place in waters, in the Red Sea.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer frames the whole story with water: The Nile at the start and the Red Sea at the end.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last three sentences of Chapter 4. Which two waters does the writer name?

exercises.title: Using the Past as a Weapon
exercises.instructions: Choose the reading the story supports.
exercises.question: The Pharaoh reminds Moses of the Nile, the palace and the Egyptian man. Why?
options: to threaten him by using his past against him
to thank him for coming back to the palace
to invite him to live again as a prince
to prove that Moses had never left Egypt
exercises.explanation: Chapter 19 says: “Moses (pbuh) knew that Pharaoh’s talk about his past, his upbringing, and the Pharaoh’s charity was his way of threatening him.” Moses answered calmly that “he had committed the act only by accident”.

feedback.correct: Yes. The Pharaoh’s kind-sounding questions were really a threat, and Moses saw through them.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence right after the Pharaoh’s questions in Chapter 19. What did Moses know about them?

exercises.title: A Secret Believer
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is supported by the story.
exercises.question: Queen Asiye fits the group that Chapter 5 describes: people who kept their belief secret.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5 says some people “kept it secret and outwardly followed social norms without opposing the Pharaoh”. Chapter 7 says of Asiye: “She was a secret believer and persuaded her husband with her words that this baby would be a ray of light for both of them!”

feedback.correct: True. Asiye hid her faith, yet she still used her words to protect Moses.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the middle of Chapter 5 with the description of Queen Asiye in Chapter 7.

exercises.title: More Than Performers
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is supported by the story.
exercises.question: The writer presents the magicians as simple entertainers, so their belief meant little to the Pharaoh.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 21 says: “At that time, magicians were not merely performers, but the elite intellectual scholars of ancient Egypt. So it was a major defeat and disappointment for the Pharaoh.”

feedback.correct: Right. When Egypt’s own scholars bowed down to Allah, the Pharaoh lost his strongest witnesses.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentences after the magicians bow down in Chapter 21. Who were the magicians at that time?

exercises.title: Words in Context
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning in the story.
exercises.question: What does each word mean where it appears?

matchingPairs.left: illusion
matchingPairs.right: something that looks real but is not

matchingPairs.left: subsided
matchingPairs.right: became weaker and calmer

matchingPairs.left: dazzled
matchingPairs.right: unable to see well because of strong light

matchingPairs.left: mobilized
matchingPairs.right: gathered and made ready for action

correctAnswer.illusion: something that looks real but is not
correctAnswer.dazzled: unable to see well because of strong light
correctAnswer.mobilized: gathered and made ready for action

exercises.explanation: Chapter 20: “However, this was only an illusion.” Chapter 16: “Moses’ fear subsided, and he felt peace”. Chapter 20: “Pharaoh’s eyes were dazzled by the brightness of the hand.” Chapter 22: “he mobilized his huge army and started following them.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Each word shows a turn in the story: a false sign, a calm heart, a true sign and an army on the move.
feedback.incorrect: Read each word in its sentence in Chapters 16, 20 and 22, and use the words around it.

exercises.title: Voices in the Story
exercises.instructions: Match each speaker with their words.
exercises.question: Who says these words in the story?

matchingPairs.left: Herodotus
matchingPairs.right: “Egypt is the gift of the Nile.”

matchingPairs.left: the quarrelsome Israelite
matchingPairs.right: “Your aim is nothing but to become a tyrant in the land”

matchingPairs.left: the man from the farthest end of the city
matchingPairs.right: “Truly, I am to you one of those who give sincere advice.”

matchingPairs.left: the Pharaoh’s callers
matchingPairs.right: “These indeed are but a small band.”

correctAnswer.Herodotus: “Egypt is the gift of the Nile.”
correctAnswer.the quarrelsome Israelite: “Your aim is nothing but to become a tyrant in the land”
correctAnswer.the man from the farthest end of the cit: “Truly, I am to you one of those who give sincere advice.”
correctAnswer.the Pharaoh’s callers: “These indeed are but a small band.”

exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: the historian Herodotus says “Egypt is the gift of the Nile.” Chapter 10: the Israelite accuses Moses: “Your aim is nothing but to become a tyrant in the land”. Chapter 11: the man warns Moses: “Truly, I am to you one of those who give sincere advice.” Chapter 22: “Then Pharaoh sent callers to all the cities, saying: ‘Truly! These indeed are but a small band.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Some voices warn, some accuse and some mock, and each shows a different view of Moses.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 3, 10, 11 and 22. Who is speaking there?

exercises.title: A Proud Community
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 2 with one word: superiority, weakness, freedom or history.
exercises.question: What did the Israelites believe because of their forefathers?
exercises.fillBlanksText: As Prophet Isaac (pbuh), Prophet Jacob (pbuh), and Prophet Joseph (pbuh) were their forefathers, the Israelites also believed in their [blank].
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2 says the Israelites “also believed in their superiority. That is why the pharaohs wanted to keep them weak.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Their sense of superiority made the pharaohs even more worried about them.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first two sentences of Chapter 2. Why did the pharaohs want to keep them weak?

exercises.title: Why They Obeyed
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 21 with one word: vision, money, courage or food.
exercises.question: Why did many Israelites ignore Moses and obey the Pharaoh?
exercises.fillBlanksText: They lacked [blank] since they had been under oppression for a long time.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 21 says: “They lacked vision since they had been under oppression for a long time. They believed that their king was wealthy and could meet all of their material needs.”

feedback.correct: Yes. “Vision” here means the ability to see beyond today’s needs, and long oppression had taken it away.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 21. What had long oppression taken from the people?

exercises.title: From the Nile to the Calf
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: How does Moses’ life unfold across the book?

sequencingItems.text: Moses discovers near Mount Sinai that he has lost his way.
The Pharaoh’s economic experts suggest killing boys only every other year.
Some Israelites ask Moses to make an idol for them.
Moses spends ten years as a shepherd in Midian.
The magicians’ ropes take the shapes of moving snakes.
The Pharaoh is astonished that the baby accepts only one woman’s milk.

exercises.explanation: The new policy (Chapter 6), the nurse (Chapter 8), Midian (Chapter 14), Mount Sinai (Chapter 15), the contest (Chapter 20) and the idol worshippers on the way to Canaan (Chapter 24).

feedback.correct: Yes. The story moves from the palace to Midian, then to the contest and the journey after the sea.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Moses lost his way on the journey back from Midian, before he met the Pharaoh again.
